articles.title: Yemen war heats up further as Hormuz stalemate persists
articles.body:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi heads to China to meet his counterpart Wang Yi as Beijing is exceedingly trying to mediate an end to the US-Israeli war
The Houthi Foreign Ministry says that navigation remains safe in the Bab al-Mandeb strait, and blames Saudi Arabia for trying to "mislead the international community". Meanwhile, fighting continues with reports of a Houthi drone downed near Mecca, and Houthis claiming that they shot down a Saudi fighter jet
US officials met representatives of Yemen's Houthis in Oman over the weekend, five sources familiar with the matter told Reuters, days after the Iran-backed militia seized a strategic stretch of the Red Sea coast in a sweeping offensive that routed Saudi-backed forces
The Trump administration is preparing to approve a $2.8bn arms package for Israel that includes 40,000 heavy bombs. At the same time, Israeli attacks are continuing on Gaza, occupied West Bank, southern Lebanon and south Syria despite any agreements or alleged ceasefires
And so we continue our live coverage...
Sweden expels Iran embassy employee, summons ambassador
Sweden said Wednesday it had expelled an Iranian embassy employee and summoned the country's ambassador, accusing Tehran of making threats against Jewish and Israeli interests in Sweden.
"We know that Iran, over a long period of time, has conducted activities that threaten security in and against Sweden, targeting both individuals who oppose the Iranian regime and various Jewish and Israeli interests in our country. This has, among other things, been done by making use of criminal networks," Justice Minister Gunnar Strommer said in a statement to AFP.
Arab League chief condemns alleged Houthi attack on Mecca
Arab League Secretary General Nabil Fahmy condemned on Wednesday an alleged attempted attack by Yemen's Houthis targeting Mecca in Saudi Arabia.
"Compromising the security of Mecca and the sanctity of Islamic holy sites is a matter of extreme gravity," he said in a statement, applauding the Saudi air force's thwarting of the attack.
He warned that Houthi attacks on Saudi territory "threaten the region's security and stability".
Yemen's Houthis say targeted Saudi oil facility, air base
Yemen's Houthis on Wednesday said they targeted an Aramco facility in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu as well as an air base in southern Saudi Arabia in response to Saudi airstrikes.
Military spokesman Yahya Saree said Saudi Arabia had launched more than 450 air strikes this week, and that in response, the Iran-backed group "targeted the Aramco facility in Yanbu with dozens of ballistic missiles and drones" causing fires, as well as "the Khamis Mushait air base".
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi rejected on Wednesday any plans for Palestinian displacement, hours after Israel's defence minister said the army would "finish the job" in Gaza and remove Palestinians.
During a visit by Palestinian president Mahmud Abbas, Sisi "reiterated Egypt's firm stance against the displacement of the Palestinian people or any attempt to annihilate the Palestinian cause".
Egypt shares the only land border with the Gaza Strip that is not controlled by Israel, and has since 2023 rejected plans to displace the territory's more than two million people into the Sinai peninsula.
Last year, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said Cairo had turned down multiple offers to forgive parts of its massive foreign debt bill in exchange for allowing mass displacement into its territory.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz on Wednesday said it was only a matter of time before Israel resumes full-scale war in Gaza, "to finish the job so that we can also implement the migration plan".
US officials met Iran-backed Houthis in Oman: Reuters
US officials met representatives of Yemen's Houthis in Oman over the weekend, five sources familiar with the matter told Reuters, days after the Iran-backed militia seized a strategic stretch of the Red Sea coast in a sweeping offensive that routed Saudi-backed forces.
The meeting, which has not been made public, was held at the US Embassy in Muscat, three of the sources said on the condition of anonymity. Two sources said that Oman's government, a longtime regional mediator, helped organise the meeting.
The Trump administration designated the Houthis a "foreign terrorist organisation" in March 2025, criminalising support for the group. But Washington has negotiated with them since, reaching a ceasefire in May last year after bombing the group for two months to halt a campaign of attacks on Red Sea shipping.
President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the Houthis had phoned his administration asking the United States to keep out of the Yemen war. Vice President JD Vance said on Monday the United States was in direct contact with the group, without giving details.
In the meeting, which one source said took place on Sunday, the Houthis told US officials that they had no intention of attacking US vessels and that they were committed to the 2025 ceasefire with the S, two sources said.
One of the sources, a Yemeni, said the militia group also said they would not attack Israeli ships or any commercial vessels, except those belonging to Saudi Arabia.
According to two of the sources, the US side was represented by embassy personnel.
One of those sources said the Houthi delegation included a senior official based in Muscat who is under US sanctions, Mohammad Abdulsalam. Another source confirmed Abdulsalam's presence along with that of another senior Houthi official, Abdelmalik al-Ajiri.
After settlements sanctions, Israel is planning a war on UK
As the UK sanctions occupied West Bank settlements, Israeli politicians and the lobby are weaponising antisemitism to defend the occupation and evade accountability, writes Richard Silverstein.
Deputy Commander of the Revolutionary Guard Naval Forces for Political Affairs, Ali Mohammadi, said that no ship in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz is outside the scope of monitoring by Iran, indicating that any ship can be targeted at any point if necessary.
He said, according to what was reported by Fars agency: "The Americans believe that they can impose surrender on us by destroying a few bridges or roads, while we were present in the most difficult weather conditions, even in places like Farsi Island, whose area is no larger than a few football fields, and our connection to the motherland was never severed."
What Greece and Israel's defence deal means for the Mideast
Greece is buying more than an air-defence system from Israel. It is deepening a strategic relationship, with implications for the wider Middle East, writes Giorgio Cafiero.
At least 20 people, including five children, died, and dozens remained missing on Wednesday after a apartment building in Gaza collapsed from damage sustained in earlier Israeli strikes, the territory's civil defence agency said, giving an updated toll.
The bodies of "20 martyrs have been recovered from the rubble of a building that collapsed... Among the dead are five infants, while dozens of people remain trapped beneath the debris," said Mahmoud Bassal, the spokesperson for the civil defence agency.
China FM says willing to 'safeguard' Iran's rights
China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi said Beijing was willing to "safeguard" Iran's rights during talks with his counterpart Abbas Araghchi on Wednesday, as Beijing seeks to mediate in Tehran's war with the United States.
China is "willing to strengthen dialogue and cooperation with Iran, and safeguard Iran's legitimate rights and interests", Wang told Araghchi as they met in the Chinese capital.
"We encourage Iran and the US to stay rational and restrained," he added.
The talks come one week before an expected trip by Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington, where he will meet US President Donald Trump.
China, a top economic partner of Iran, has long sought a detente in the months-long conflict in the Middle East, which has at times spilled over into neighbouring countries.
"We do not wish to see regional tensions spilling over into Yemen and the Red Sea," Wang said.
Saudi Arabia calls an attempted Mecca attack a 'red line'
Saudi Arabia accused Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels overnight of trying to attack Islam’s holiest city, prompting condemnation from countries in the region but no sign of military support. The kingdom, a key US ally, declared Mecca a "red line" as it slid deeper into the new front of the Iran war.
The Houthis denied firing drones toward Mecca, about 1,100 kilometers (680 miles) from Yemen’s border. The Saudis said they intercepted and destroyed the drone before it entered the airspace over the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad.
Lebanon wants Israel security deal, Hezbollah disarmament
Speaking ahead of his departure to France on Wednesday, President Joseph Aoun told AFP Lebanon wanted a new force, European or otherwise, to prevent a security vacuum after UN peacekeepers leave south Lebanon when their mandate expires at the end of the year.
He called on the United States, European Union and Arab countries to support Lebanon's military as it deploys across the south.
In Paris, Aoun will attend a meeting hosted by President Emmanuel Macron and attended by King Abdullah II of Jordan to build international support for Lebanese troops as they deploy across the country.
"What matters is that there is no vacuum," Aoun told AFP on Tuesday. He added that any new force for Lebanon's south, part of which is occupied by Israel, would be "temporary until the (Lebanese) army can deploy".
"Whatever the nature of this force, that poses no problem for me: European, non-European, American, another United Nations force, Asian, or even a mix of European, Arab and Asian forces," Aoun said.
"The best and most optimal option remains extending UNIFIL's mandate," he added.
Aoun also said he wants a security agreement with Israel "primarily to end the state of hostility and the deployment of the army on the border. This could be a prelude to a later peace agreement, but we cannot jump directly to a peace agreement".
"We have no choice but negotiations, because the alternative is war, which would be very costly for us," Aoun added.
Aoun reiterated Lebanon was determined to disarm the Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah, saying the decision was "neither negotiable nor open to discussion".
However, he said, "the objective is not a confrontation... We are determined to resolve this issue peacefully. "This is not about building a state at the cost of a bloody conflict... or a new civil war."
"The best and most optimal option remains extending UNIFIL's mandate," Aoun added. [Getty]
Washington fired 70 missiles to repel Iran attack on Jordan
The Wall Street Journal reported, citing US and regional officials, that the US military fired up to 70 or more of its advanced interceptor missiles for air defense last week in response to the Iranian rocket attack on Jordan, noting that this massive expenditure is evidence of Iran’s improved ability to target US forces and challenge its air defenses.
Some officials said US forces fired between 60 and 70 Patriot interceptor missiles to counter the attack, including about 20 ballistic missiles. The Americans also fired more than 12 THAAD interceptor missiles, according to one official. Another official explained that this expenditure is roughly equivalent to what the United States has spent in an entire week during other periods of the war.
War-damaged Gaza building collapses killing 12 people
Gaza rescuers on Wednesday combed through the wreckage of a bombed-out apartment building that collapsed overnight, killing at least 12 Palestinians, including five children, and trapping dozens of others beneath the rubble.
The incident highlights the ongoing danger for tens of thousands of Palestinians who live in an estimated 2,000 damaged buildings due to Israeli airstrikes across Gaza.
Rescue workers from the civil defense said at least 12 people, including five children, were killed and 14 others injured when the seven-storey building collapsed.
Nearly 100 more people were believed to be trapped under the rubble, around 50 are believed to be children.
The United States hammered home a message touting its energy dominance at Tuesday's meeting of G20 energy ministers in Houston, while brushing past the consequences of Washington's war in Iran and environmental concerns.
The meeting's slogan to "Unleash the full potential of American energy" has been repeated by US officials tirelessly in Texas since the gathering kicked off Monday.
Members of US President Donald Trump's cabinet say his policies are a reversal of his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden, with Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) chief Lee Zeldin accusing Biden of participating in "climate alarmism" by promoting renewable energies.
"The whole idea was to produce enough energy for prosperity at home, but to be able to provide secure, affordable, reliable energy for all of our allies," Interior Secretary Doug Bergum said.
To help meet the growing demand for electricity, driven by the needs of the artificial intelligence industry, the EPA announced a reduction in limits on pollution from gas- and coal-fired power plants, sparking outcry from environmentalists.
Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned on Wednesday "in the strongest possible terms the dastardly and heinous" attack on Mecca, which a Saudi-led coalition blamed on Yemen's Houthis.
"The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act," he said on X.
The Houthis have denied attacking Islam's holy city.
Israel will 'finish job' in Gaza and 'remove Palestinians'
Israel's defence minister said Wednesday it was only a matter of time before the country resumes full-scale war in Gaza and moves to force out its two million Palestinians—a war crime.
Israel Katz, who is known for xenophobic and horrific remarks, was responding to criticism from another right-wing contender ahead of 27 October elections.
Katz said 70 percent of Gaza had already been emptied of its population by the Israeli war.
He said that an October 2025 ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump had "supreme value for all Israelis" by leading to the return of remaining hostages and ensuring "a commitment by the United States" to disarming Hamas.
"We all understand that this is not going to happen—and the IDF is prepared, once given the directive to eliminate Hamas, to finish the job so that we can also implement the migration plan," Katz said in a statement, referring to the Israeli military.
He said earlier this month that Israel was ready to remove Palestinians from Gaza by sea and land but was waiting for the United States, which he said was discussing where the two million people would go.
Nearly all of Gaza's population has been internally displaced and most of the territory lies in rubble after the war.
Forcibly displacing a population under occupation is consider a war crime and crime against humanity.
The war with Iran cost the US military around $38 billion as of August 1, the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office said Tuesday, with billions more potentially added to the price tag each month the conflict wears on.
"As of August 1, 2026, the armed conflict with Iran has cost (the Department of Defense) approximately $38 billion," said the CBO in a report, referring to the war that started after US-Israeli strikes targeting Iran from late February.
It added that depending on the intensity of violence, costs per month could range between $2-$3 billion or more if the conflict continued.
The overall figures reflect the cost of replacing expended munitions and equipment lost in battle and increased fuel costs for the military, among other factors, the report said.
The price of replacing munitions used through August 1 was estimated at $21.7 billion, with CBO noting that such replacements have been the largest single component of costs incurred by the Defense Department in the conflict.
The "main opportunity cost" for the department meanwhile has been the depletion of missile defense interceptors, leaving the United States with reduced inventory for several years.
Comparing the reported expenditures of missile defense interceptors with total numbers the department has bought suggests the United States "has probably used between one-half and two-thirds of its inventory of those munitions since June 2025," the CBO warned.
For a third time, the US House has voted to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution that would halt President Donald Trump's ability to continue military action without congressional approval.
The roll call late Tuesday, 220-204, was similar to earlier efforts this summer, with a few more Republicans joining all Democrats voting to bring an end to the conflict. None of the resolutions have made it to the president's desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto the measure.
"Remember when Donald Trump said that this war would last just a few weeks?" said Rep. Seth Moulton, D-Mass., who served as a Marine during the Iraq War and pushed the resolution forward.
He said it's time for Congress to "actually ask tough questions, as the Constitution directs us to do, rather than be subservient to another warmongering administration."
Yemen's Houthis on Wednesday said they shot down a Saudi fighter jet, claiming a locally made munition was used to target the warplane.
"The Yemeni Armed Forces, with Allah's aid and grace, succeeded in shooting down a Saudi F15 fighter jet while it was carrying out hostile operations in support of its military mobilisations in the airspace of Marib province," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on social media, while accusing Saudi Arabia of launching 450 strikes.
He said the jet had been targeted "using a locally made air-to-air missile".
The spokesman also dismissed Saudi claims that the Houthis had targeted the holy city of Mecca this week.
"Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites," he said.
The Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces since Yemen's civil war reignited in July.
The group have also declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and have been targeting its ships in the Red Sea.
In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of the entirety of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
The strait has become vital to Saudi crude exports as the wider Middle East war chokes the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

articles.title: US burns through dozens of missile interceptors in single Iranian attack on Jordan: Report
articles.body:
Busra Nur Cakmak
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
The US military used as many as 70 Patriot interceptors and more than a dozen THAAD anti-missile interceptors to counter a recent Iranian ballistic missile attack on Jordan, highlighting growing pressure on American air defense stocks, The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday.
US forces fired between 60 and 70 Patriot interceptors against an attack involving about 20 ballistic missiles, while more than a dozen Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors were also launched, the newspaper reported, citing US and regional officials familiar with the matter.
The number of interceptors expended was roughly equivalent to what US forces have used during an entire week at other points in the conflict, according to the report.
Iran reportedly used warheads that separated into multiple projectiles as they approached their targets, complicating efforts to intercept them.
The defenses did not stop all incoming threats, with Iran striking fighter jets and other aircraft at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, though no US personnel were killed in the latest attack, the Journal said.
Iranian attacks have become increasingly complex during the conflict, employing different missile types, trajectories, maneuvers and warheads in attempts to penetrate US defenses, officials told the newspaper.
US Central Command declined to comment on the report, while the Pentagon rejected suggestions that American munitions were depleted.
“Reports suggesting that the United States’ munitions are depleted are completely false,” Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said, adding that the US military remains capable of responding to threats.
President Donald Trump also said Monday that the US maintains large stocks of interceptors and is increasing production.
The Defense Department's inspector general, however, said in a report this week that the conflict “has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply.”
By mid-July, the US had used about 1,700 Patriot interceptors and more than 200 THAAD interceptors during the conflict, according to officials cited by the Journal. US Navy ships had additionally fired about 150 Standard Missile interceptors against Iranian missiles and drones.
Lockheed Martin, which manufactures Patriot interceptors, produced 620 in 2025 and is seeking to increase annual production to roughly 2,000, according to the report.
US officials have also expressed concerns that the transfer of large quantities of munitions to the Middle East could affect Washington's ability to respond to potential threats elsewhere, including in Europe and the Indo-Pacific.
Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of US Central Command, separately told CBS' “60 Minutes” this week that he was not concerned about interceptor shortages and that US forces were prepared for any contingency.
The pressure on interceptor inventories has also prompted Gulf states to seek additional air defense munitions after months of Iranian missile and drone attacks, while affecting the availability of systems for Ukraine's defense against Russian strikes, according to the Journal.

articles.title: Lithuanian MEP: Europe must stop being afraid to respond – opinion
articles.body:
Russia’s hybrid war against Europe did not begin with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, nor in recent years. The Kremlin intelligence services have been conducting hostile operations across Europe since Vladimir Putin came to power.
For too long, Europe has failed to respond adequately. Some worried that a stronger response would provoke Moscow. But the opposite has happened. The Kremlin interprets hesitation and fear of escalation as weakness, inviting further aggression. Every weak response teaches the Kremlin that it can test the next boundary, create more disruption and chaos inside our societies without facing consequences serious enough to change its behaviour. Putin goes as far as he is allowed to go. Fear of escalation has not prevented escalation: it has further encouraged it.
Europe is a target of Russian hybrid warfare that is becoming increasingly less hybrid. It combines military and non-military tools often designed to remain below the threshold of open armed conflict, including cyber operations, disinformation, economic coercion, sabotage and weaponising migration. The line between hybrid and conventional warfare has blurred. We hear daily about acts of sabotage and sabotage attempts on our infrastructure and drones violating our airspace and even being laden with explosives, like in Leipzig. Around elections, Russian cyberattacks, and disinformation campaigns intensify. GPS jamming and spoofing are everyday occurrences in Europe’s eastern border regions.
Russia remains the primary threat to Europe’s democratic integrity. It targets us through information manipulation and hybrid interference. By deploying hundreds of thousands of fake social media accounts, particularly around elections, it seeks to influence people’s minds, portray Russia as strong and invincible, and amplify narratives and candidates favourable to the Kremlin.
Russia does not act alone: it has partners in authoritarian states such as Belarus, China, Iran and North Korea. Belarus, for example, has weaponised migration at the EU’s borders, with over 36,000 coordinated crossing attempts recorded in 2024. In the Baltic Sea, Chinese-linked vessels have been involved in incidents damaging critical data and electricity cables.
Russia, its allies and its proxies must face real consequences, not just condemnation. We need a common threat picture, stronger tools, greater preparedness, real operational capacity and the will to use them. Any violation of a member state’s sovereignty must be met with effective retaliatory measures.
EU member states have yet to develop a coordinated response to hybrid warfare nationally, at European level and, where relevant, with NATO.
Europe’s eastern flank is its first line of defence, and we need faster implementation of the Eastern Flank Watch, an EU initiative intended to strengthen surveillance and defence along the bloc’s borders with Russia and Belarus.
We must also introduce tougher rules for Russian passport holders entering the EU. The minimum is to ban entry for anyone serving in Russian security and intelligence organisations, including former members who have fought in Ukraine.
The EU must use its economic and diplomatic power to stop the de facto Russian fleet from operating and bypassing sanctions. The owners and operators of these ships must be penalised. Furthermore, the consequences for damaging critical underwater infrastructure (CUI) must be significantly increased to serve as an effective deterrent.
We need better intelligence-sharing, more resources to counter disinformation and stronger protection of our critical infrastructure. But most of all we need sanctions that hit Russia’s economy at the heart.
Since the beginning of Russia’s attack on Ukraine, the EPP Group demanded decisive sanctions, but the Council’s step-by-step approach was slow, and the Russian economy had time to adapt. Kremlin propaganda claims sanctions do not work. This is false. Sanctions do work but require stronger enforcement and bolder measures.
In July, EU adopted 21st package of sanctions against Russia. By the end of the year, Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) will be banned from the EU and pipeline gas imports will be phased out by 30 September 2027. The European parliament strengthened the European Commission’s initial proposal towards a ban on oil and its products, ending long-term contracts sooner than originally proposed.
These are welcome decisions, but more must be done. The European Parliament’s proposals are set out in the report that the plenary adopted on 16 September. Europe can be strong if it wants to. But this resolve is challenged by a huge, lying Russian propaganda machinery.
European leaders must stop fearing the measures needed to defend our security. Today, Ukraine is an example of the will to defend and to win. So are Moldova and Armenia, which have faced massive hybrid attacks using every tool in Moscow’s arsenal, and whose leaders and people have nevertheless stood firm.
Rasa Juknevičienė is an MEP from Lithuania, EP rapporteur on Hybrid warfare

articles.title: The winter that will reach Russia's rear
articles.body:
The winter that will reach Russia's rear
Cars queue at a Gazpromneft gas station in the suburbs of Moscow, in Istra, Russia, on July 10, 2026. (Contributor / Getty Images)
Liubov Tsybulska
Director of Join Ukraine
In late August and early September, it began to look as though Russia was winning the exchange of strikes.
According to Zelensky, in late August, jet-powered drones made up more than half of all unmanned aerial vehicles launched. Ukraine shoots them down at a rate of six in ten, compared with more than nine in ten for propeller-driven ones.
There is almost nothing to shoot down ballistic missiles with: the interception rate was 40% in June and 15% in July; on the night of Aug. 1, Russia launched 27 ballistic missiles at Ukraine, with Kyiv as the main target, and only one was shot down.
According to an estimate by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, U.S. stocks of PAC-3 MSE interceptors have shrunk almost threefold as a result of combat operations against Iran.
In late August, the capital went through 13 air raid alerts in a single day.
The winter ahead may be the hardest of the full-scale war. Russia will once again try to make life in large cities impossible: electricity, water, heating, and food. The calculation is the same as in 2022: to make Ukraine break. Against this backdrop, it is fairly easy to fall into a funk. But the situation is not so one-sided.
On the night of Aug. 12, Novorossiysk was under attack for eight hours. The next day, the Russian regional communities we track published more than 300 posts about it.
In 112 of the 300, the story was about civilian deaths; in 98, about damaged buildings; in 29, about a collapsed overpass. Ships came up in only eight.
The frigates "Admiral Makarov" and "Admiral Essen," whose launchers, according to an analysis of satellite imagery, were likely knocked out of action by the strikes and fires, were not mentioned by anyone at all. Nor does the Russian reader ever hear about the shutdown of three grain terminals that previously handled exports of around 25 million tons of Russian grain.
Why do we bring up this example? Ukraine focuses on targets that matter for stopping the Russian war machine. Russians, meanwhile, see in their information environment almost nothing but what matters to them personally.
Russians feel the hardships of war before analysts do.
In our databases, which cover around a thousand regional Telegram and VKontakte communities, the fuel topic grew by 85% over the four weeks of August: hours-long lines in Perm, purchase limits in Moscow, "gasoline availability maps" as the most in-demand of all digital services.
Despite the large number of successful strikes on facilities in Russia's rear throughout August, practically none of them became a nationwide topic in Russia (as Wildberries did in July).
Russians rally around a topic in the information space only when their own skin is in the game: the most reactions and comments still go to the same Wildberries and Ozon — everyone wants to know what will happen to deliveries and whether their parcels have burned.
The social distance between Russian regions is so great that the explosions in Novorossiysk were of little interest even to residents of relatively nearby Stavropol.
Of course, strikes on Russia's rear provoke anger. But it is not aimed where the Kremlin would like it to be.
Anti-Ukrainian jabs in the comments under posts about the strikes are consistently few: 5–7% in both July and August, and that counts any mention of Ukraine at all, while outright hatred along the lines of "khokhly" (a slur for Ukrainians) is two to three times rarer.
Roughly the same share of comments is addressed to their own authorities and air defenses, and, across individual events, that share ranges from 10–16%.
The most upvoted comment under one of the posts about the already mentioned attack on Novorossiysk: "We hit them, they hit us. And for the sake of protecting facilities, complete disregard for people's safety." The second most popular: "If they can't protect us, let them wrap up this Special Military Operation. Meanwhile, all the air defense and electronic warfare systems around Moscow are lined up several rows deep."
Attention to the other August strikes was distributed the same way.
The strikes on the Syzran oil refinery were discussed almost exclusively in Samara Oblast, and the governor never named the plant.
The plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, which makes propellant for "Smerch" and "Tornado-S" multiple rocket launchers, exists in the feeds only as "5 dead in Rostov Oblast."
The strike on the "Sivash" drilling rig in the Black Sea, where Russians had placed surveillance equipment, was not mentioned even once.
The only strike to become a nationwide topic was the one on Koledino, Wildberries' largest warehouse, damaged by a strike and fire on August 16: 38% of reactions under posts about it were the angry emoji, a record for our monitoring.
The result of this systematic work: oil refining in Russia fell in August to an average of 3.8 million barrels per day, the lowest level in 20 years, no matter what Putin said about "only 10% of the oil refineries still left to repair"; the gasoline export ban has been extended to Jan. 31, 2027, and since Sept. 1, gas stations have been allowed to sell Euro-2, a fuel that can damage modern cars.
So let's go back to where we started.
Russia will bet on terror and on making survival in Ukraine's large cities impossible in winter. That means strikes on energy, water supply, warehouses of food, medicine, and essential goods, and gas stations. It is absolutely clear that this winter will be extremely difficult.
But we have been through something like this before. This will be the fourth hard winter, and the country knows roughly what to prepare for. Betting that this time it will not hold out, after three previous attempts, is a dubious investment.
We know a hard winter awaits us. But for the first time in this war, Ukraine can respond at least roughly in kind.
For Russia, however, this will be the first winter in which its rear is this vulnerable. There has never been such depth before, nor such numbers.
As for the depth, in August, Ukrainian drones reached Tobolsk, 1,900 kilometers (1,180 miles) away, and twelve large oil refineries were hit within the month. And on Sept. 9, according to the Special Operations Forces, their drones reached Novy Urengoy and the Purovsky plant in Yamal, more than 3,000 kilometers (1,864 miles) from the border; the previous record, Omsk in July, was 2,500 kilometers (1553 miles).
This is the heart of Russian gas production, which until now was considered a safe rear area.
Now numbers are also hitting records. The Russian Defense Ministry itself claims a record 1,671 drones allegedly shot down in a single day, and the mayor of Moscow reports 8,670 drones in August headed toward the Moscow region, compared with 6,225 in July.
Defending such a vast territory is impossible.
We know a hard winter awaits us. But for the first time in this war, Ukraine can respond at least roughly in kind.
How delighted Russian society will be with its own hard winter remains an open question. Judging by the comments, not very.
On Aug. 18, when more than 600 drones were flying toward Moscow, two comments under a "Moskva 24" post collected more than 800 likes each: "They fly in every day, it's no longer treated as an emergency, it's taken like the rain. Look where it's got us — couldn't just live in peace!"
And: "Are we really getting used to what's happening... or are we just ceasing to notice how our idea of normal life is changing?"
In Samara, where missiles struck on Aug. 15, the most popular reply is shorter: "We've got no damn air defense at all. They only protect Moscow."
Moscow, the Russians will probably manage to defend through the winter. The rest of Russia, they won't.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

articles.title: The West has tried everything except ending the war
articles.body:
On 6 May 2022, I began using the term tsunami of ripple effects to describe the cost of not intervening in a war that threatens the security of the Alliance. That was NATO's own strategic ambition—right up until the Madrid Summit in June 2022, where it found its political will and military capabilities wanting, deterred by Russia.
The latest wave of that tsunami reached American voters this month, in the price of diesel—and the US President's response shows exactly how the refusal to end the war keeps compounding its costs.
Diesel, and the president who blamed the victim
President Trump has urged President Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks are "hurting the world" as fuel-supply disruptions from the Ukraine and Iran wars propel US diesel prices to a record high, according to CNBC.
"Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump said during an official visit to Ireland. "Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel because he's causing a shortage of diesel. This isn't done by the Middle East; this is done by what's happening with Russia and Ukraine."
The claim inverts the evidence. The latest IEA assessment is unusually clear: the US-Iran war and the disruption of Middle Eastern flows are the dominant shock, with Gulf refined-product exports down almost 60% since February.
Disruptions to Russia's refining system and the near-halt in Russian product exports following intensified Ukrainian attacks, the IEA says, "have compounded these losses." The aggressor is responsible for the dominant shock; the war Trump himself helped start accounts for most of the rest; and the victim's attempt to force Russia toward peace has only reinforced the consequences of that aggression.
Yet Trump singled out Zelenskyy—not Putin for starting the war, not himself and Prime Minister Netanyahu for the war against Iran.
Ukraine has intensified the tempo of its refinery-strike campaign and improved its targeting to cause maximum pain to the Russian oil industry, striking at least 26 different Russian oil refineries since the beginning of 2026, according to ISW. The strikes have put roughly half of Russia's refining capacity offline and prompted widespread fuel shortages, with Moscow recently extending a ban on diesel exports through the end of September to stabilize domestic supplies.
The lie, the contradiction, and the lack of credibility
Trump's statement is an outright lie—the link to the US/Israel war on Iran is clear for anyone to see—and it is in direct contradiction with US and European policy.
As late as early July, Trump noted that Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries were an escalation capable of bringing the war to an end. The reversal appears driven primarily by the fuel-price shock and its political consequences—not by any change in his assessment of the strikes' military value. US consumers have seen a roughly 20% increase in diesel prices in a matter of weeks, midterms are seven weeks away, and the Republican Party is struggling in the polls.
And Ukraine's strikes aim at the exact effect Western sanctions were designed to achieve: ensuring Russia cannot afford to continue the war by undermining its economy. Neither the US nor Europe is supposed to import Russian crude or refined products—the EU banned them, cutting Russia's share of EU oil imports from 25.8% in 2021 to 2.2% in 2025, and the US prohibited them in March 2022.
"The United States is taking sweeping action against Russia's key source of revenue for funding its brutal and illegal war against Ukraine," Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen said in January 2025. That is exactly what Ukraine is doing—with the difference that when Ukraine does it, Trump calls it "hurting the world."
The tsunami of ripple effects
Diesel is only the latest wave. During the year after Madrid, I watched the West take the role of bystander to a war that is all about us—a Russian ever-escalating hybrid war against European NATO members—seemingly accepting the global consequences.
I say seemingly because it makes no sense to sit idle while the tsunami grows to the point where it causes political, economic, and geopolitical chain reactions impossible to predict and difficult to control.
Inaction is not neutral. It is also a choice, and it carries the consequences of engagement with one crucial difference: inaction makes us react to the strategic environment, whereas action lets us shape it.
Aid without an endpoint is not a policy for ending the war; it is a policy for enduring it.
Enduring it is what produced the tsunami: the reverberations that raise the cost of living, undermine food and energy security, and spread famine, recession, inflation, and rising interest rates—increasing the risk of social unrest, extremism, and, ultimately, the fall of governments. Europe is living through the biggest refugee crisis since the Second World War.
he international security architecture is being dismantled, the institutions meant to unite us are discredited, and NATO no longer deters Russia—raising the risk of direct conflict between Russia and Europe.
In June 2023, I argued this would likely change the political landscape in the US and Europe—as in the 1930s—as political forces sought to exploit voters' frustration over the war's global effects. It produced President Trump and a rising tide of right-wing forces across Europe—the leading edge of what Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called, at Davos, a rupture the world hasn't yet reckoned with: "We understand that this rupture calls for more than adaptation. It calls for honesty about the world as it is... We know the old order is not coming back." Its consequences for Europe have not yet dawned on us.
How to end it
The only way to end the tsunami of ripple effects is to end the war. Waiting only lets it reach the scale where it produces chain reactions impossible to control.
Since 2014, the West has tried to stop Russia's war through diplomacy, negotiations and ceasefires; sanctions and economic pressure; diplomatic isolation; military aid, training and intelligence; NATO deterrence and reinforcement; and humanitarian and financial assistance. More than 200 negotiations were held to stop the war from happening.
They were all futile, because Russia was never negotiating in good faith—it sees negotiation as a means to defeat its opponents. Insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results.
For a negotiation to succeed, it must solve the cause of the war: Russia's Great Power ambitions, its pursuit of strategic parity with the US and China at the expense of its neighbours. Until that is checked, there will be no peace—and those ambitions are not negotiable. They can only be denied through military power.
The West has done everything short of military intervention. It is time to employ military power, because the cost of continuing the present path is far too high. If Europe wants to turn the tide, it must become proactive. Instead of waiting for the war more intelligence services are warning about, Europe—or rather a Coalition of Like-Minded European countries—must help shift Russia's appraisal of the strategic environment. We need to intervene militarily to end the war, and the tsunami of ripple effects with it.

articles.body:

Ukraine Exposes 54 Russian Firms Behind Iskander and Zircon Missiles
Ukraine’s military intelligence has disclosed information on 54 Russian companies linked to the production of electronic warfare systems, military aircraft electronics, drones, and components for Iskander-M and Zircon missiles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) on September 15, the companies are part of or managed by Concern Radio-Electronic Technologies (KRET), a subsidiary of Russia’s state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec. The information was published through HUR’s War&Sanctions database.
KRET companies primarily develop and manufacture electronic warfare equipment, identification friend-or-foe systems, and onboard electronics used by Russian fighter jets and helicopters, HUR said.
Their production also includes electric motors, navigation and control systems for drones, counter-drone equipment, and remotely operated machine-gun platforms.
HUR identified several KRET companies as participants in Russia’s missile supply chain. The Stavropol-based Signal plant manufactures and supplies S200A1 compact jamming stations for 9M723 ballistic missiles used by the Iskander-M system.
The Kaluga Scientific Research Radio Engineering Institute, another company within the KRET network, supplies components for the 3B228 electronic protection system installed on Russia’s 3M22 Zircon missiles, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
HUR also said KRET’s central organization provides financing to cover shortfalls in Russian state defense contracts carried out by companies within the concern.
Of the 54 companies disclosed by Ukrainian intelligence, 19 are currently not sanctioned by any country participating in the international sanctions coalition.
Among them is Inertial Technologies of Technocomplex, which HUR identified as a manufacturer of strapdown inertial navigation systems for Kh-59M2 and Kh-59M2A guided air-launched missiles and Orion unmanned aircraft systems.
The Tambov Elektropribor plant, also not covered by coalition sanctions, supplies gyroscopes for 9M727 cruise missiles used by the Iskander system. The Ulan-Ude Instrument-Making Production Association produces aircraft automation equipment, radio-navigation systems, and electric motors for drones, according to HUR.
KRET is the tenth Rostec holding whose corporate network has been published by Ukrainian intelligence through the War&Sanctions portal. The database now contains information on 764 companies associated with the Russian state corporation.
Earlier, on September 9, Ukraine’s military intelligence said it had breached the Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology, a key Russian missile developer behind the Yars, Bulava, Iskander-M, and Oreshnik systems, obtaining data on the institute’s structure, projects, and 2,648 employees.

articles.title: Poland reaffirms support for Ukraine after drone strikes
articles.body:
Poland reaffirms support for Ukraine after drone strikes
September 16, 2026
Russia's war against Ukraine is moving ever closer to the border with Poland.
After a drone attack by Russia destroyed a gas station and the locomotive of a passenger train near the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing between Poland and Ukraine early Sunday, Warsaw has demonstrated its determination in the face of the immediate threat.
"Border crossings in Poland — as has previously been the case in Moldova and Romania — are being targeted in an attempt to discourage people and deter countries from supporting Ukraine," Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told the private broadcaster TVN on Monday.
"Support for Ukraine is part of Poland's reason of state," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. He added that Poland's own security situation would be worsened should Ukraine lose the war.
Poland prepares response
Early on Monday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk met with the ministers responsible for Poland's security. Senior military commanders also attended the meeting. "We discussed further measures to strengthen the security of our borders," Tusk subsequently wrote on the social media platform X.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski provided more details.
"Poland will provide a nonprovocative but serious response to Russia's escalation, such as the attack on the train in Ukraine near the Polish border, one that will strengthen security," Poland's top diplomat told TVN Monday evening.
On Sunday, Tusk spoke of an "escalation of activities" by Russia. The prime minister also announced that he would discuss the incident with Poland's allies in Europe.
"There is no doubt that we, if necessary, must be prepared, together with them, to deliver a coordinated response," Tusk said after a special session of the Government Centre for Security.
Drone attack on Kyiv-Warsaw train
Russian drones attacked a passenger train on the Kyiv-Warsaw line just short of the Polish border on Sunday morning. The train's locomotive was destroyed in the attack. All passengers and crew were evacuated in time.
Two special trains carrying high-profile participants returning from a security conference in Kyiv were nearby at almost the same time as the attack.
Among those on board were former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, former Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin, former Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski and Günter Sautter, foreign and security policy adviser to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Polish political scientist Katarzyna Piskorska, who has organized the Warsaw Security Forum in the Polish capital for years, was also on the train.
"Our train was stopped beforehand, and the passengers were evacuated," she told TVN. "The situation was very tense, but everyone remained calm. We were given an evacuation plan and knew exactly what to do."
"The Russians wanted to intimidate us, but they achieved the opposite: The participants affected by this incident are determined to step up their support for the country that was attacked," she said.
Piskorska said the mood in Ukraine was "worse than at any time since the start of the war." She pointed to a new generation of drones equipped with jet engines that can reach their targets much faster.
Support for Ukraine slipping in Poland
Despite numerous acts of sabotage assumed to have be carried out by Russian agents and incidents involving Russian missiles and drones, Poland's government has remained firm in its commitment to supporting Ukraine.
Foreign Minister Sikorski has even called for support for Ukraine to be doubled, arguing that doing so is in Poland's own security interest.
But the government in Warsaw also has to consider the shift in Polish public opinion.
In a survey conducted in mid-July, 52% of respondents said they were in favor of continued military aid for Kyiv; 45% opposed it. These figures stood at 77.5% and 18.3%, respectively, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"Russia has won the propaganda war in Poland," Piskorska said. "It is absurd that we are taking the side of the aggressor and claiming that this is not our war," she said, appealing to fellow Poles to "finally wake up."
Defense Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz has also expressed concern about what he described as a "radical shift in sentiment."
"In the past, there was consensus on this issue. Today, we are seeing great skepticism toward Ukraine," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "There are forces in Poland that are spreading Russian propaganda," he added.
Polish media sound alarm
The Polish media, too, are sounding the alarm.
"Putin is sending out a signal that he is prepared to kill our citizens," Bartosz Wielinski wrote in the Tuesday edition of the Polish daily Gazeta Wyborcza. The Kremlin, he wrote, had sent a message that Poland is "the next country in line."
"These are no longer arson attacks or cyberattacks. These are acts on the threshold of war," he wrote.
Polish daily Rzeczpospolita said that "Putin is knocking on NATO's door."
"The attack on the Warsaw–Kyiv railway line was not just another Russian provocation. It was an attempt to intimidate Poland and the West. The response from Poland's politicians will show whether they are capable of assuming responsibility for the country's security," wrote editor-in-chief Michal Szuldrzynski.
Incidents involving Russian drones are now almost a daily occurrence in Poland. On Monday, a drone washed up on a beach near Jaroslawiec on the Baltic coast. A preliminary investigation indicates that the aircraft was unarmed and appeared to be intended for reconnaissance rather than combat.
"We do not know where Russia believes the limits of the escalation spiral lie," Kosiniak-Kamysz said. "But we do know that the Russians are prepared to go even further."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: New interceptors for Russian jet-powered drones 'successfully tested,' Zelensky says
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: New interceptors for Russian jet-powered drones 'successfully tested,' Zelensky says
Key developments on Sept. 15:
- Ukraine has 'successfully tested' new interceptor against Russian jet-powered drones, Zelensky says
- Russia launches drone attack on Kyiv, killing at least 1, injuring 12
- Russia suffers over 300,000 military losses in Ukraine since start of 2026, General Staff says
- Belarus holds 'defensive' military drills near borders with Poland, Lithuania
Ukraine has "successfully" trialed another interceptor drone designed to target Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sept. 15 following a briefing by Ukrainian Armed Forces Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi.
As Russia expands its arsenal of Shahed-type jet-powered drones, including the Geran-3, Geran-4, and Geran-5, and the cruise missile-like Banderol loitering munition, Ukraine is facing mounting difficulties intercepting the weapons during prolonged attacks, with Kyiv and the surrounding region frequently targeted.
"A 'shahed' was hit successfully, but some aspects of controlling the interceptor still need to be refined. The work continues – it will take some more time," Zelensky wrote on X.
The jet-powered drones can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour (nearly 370 miles per hour), making them more difficult to intercept than earlier, piston-powered Shahed variants. Their use also increased sharply this summer, rising roughly fivefold in July compared with June, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said Aug. 31.
Russia launched nearly 800 jet-powered drones toward Ukraine over four days in late August, according to Zelensky.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said Aug. 29 that Ukraine had field-tested four potential interceptors against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, without specifying which companies were developing them or how far along the projects were.
Anatolii Hrapchynskyi, deputy director of an electronic warfare company and a reserve Air Force officer, told the Kyiv Independent that the use of jet-powered drones was to be expected as Russian forces had been seeking ways to overwhelm Ukraine's anti-aircraft defenses.

Russia launches drone attack on Kyiv, killing at least 1, injuring 12
Russian forces attacked Kyiv on the morning of Sept. 15, killing one person and injuring at least 12 others, local authorities said.
Kyiv City Military Administration reported at 8:39 a.m. local time that a Russian drone had crashed at a petrol station in the Holosiivskyi district of the capital.
Another gas station in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district was hit at around 6 a.m. local time, according to Mayor Vitali Klitschko. One person was hospitalized in critical condition and later died in hospital, according to the mayor.
As of 10 a.m. local time, seven people had been injured in the morning attacks on Kyiv, while two of those wounded were hospitalized in serious condition, Klitschko said.
As of 5 p.m. local time, six of the injured remain hospitalized, Klitschko said.
Six of the injured were in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, where a non-residential building was damaged in the early hours of Sept. 15, Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported.
Russia's attack also damaged the data center of BeMobile, according to Ukraine's National Paralympic Committee, whose website was temporarily unavailable following the morning strike.
The committee said emergency restoration work was underway and that it was awaiting the resumption of services by its partner company, UCloud.
The Kyiv Independent contacted UCloud, which confirmed that its Kyiv data center had been affected by the Russian attack.
The company did not specify the nature or extent of the damage, but said the affected websites were expected to resume operation within "several hours."
According to preliminary reports, there were also strikes on warehouses in the city's Obolonskyi district, Klitschko said.
read also
Russia suffers over 300,000 military losses in Ukraine since start of 2026, General Staff says
Russian forces have lost 301,030 troops killed and wounded since the beginning of 2026, Ukraine's General Staff said on Sept. 15.
The statement comes after the summer campaign on the battlefield in Ukraine ended, with Russian losses exceeding 1.5 million since the start of the full-scale invasion.
The General Staff said nearly 300,000 losses were roughly equivalent to the personnel strength of 150 motorized rifle regiments, based on an estimated 2,000 troops per regiment.
"The enemy's significant losses are the result of effective combat operations by all components of the Ukrainian Defense Forces," the General Staff said.
Since the beginning of 2026, Russian forces have suffered around 30,000 casualties per month in Ukraine.
The largest losses were recorded during the three summer months, when Russia suffered 124,170 military casualties, the General Staff said. In July alone, the figure surged to a record 42,860 — the highest monthly toll since the start of the full-scale war. In August, the monthly figure again topped 40,000.
"Such high Russian casualties are primarily linked to their tactics. They continue to deploy infantry — often in waves — in an attempt to overwhelm our positions with sheer numbers. At the same time, manpower remains one of their primary tools for achieving results," electronic warfare operator 'Strada,' who asked to be identified by callsign only for security reasons, told the Kyiv Independent.
In September, Russia has already lost 20,360 troops as of the morning of Sept. 15, the General Staff said.
read also
Belarus holds 'defensive' military drills near borders with Poland, Lithuania
Belarus is holding military exercises near its borders with Poland and Lithuania from Sept. 15-18, the Belarusian Defense Ministry said on Sept. 15.
The Belarusian Defense Ministry described the drills as "defensive" and said they are aimed at improving the military's ability to "protect the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity."
The exercise is focused on preparing troops to conduct a "strategic military operation," including securing the border, countering alleged sabotage and reconnaissance groups, and combating drones and light aircraft.
Exercises are being held at the Gozhsky training ground in Grodno Oblast, around 6 kilometers (4 miles) from the Lithuanian border, as well as at the Brestsky and Ruzhansky training grounds, roughly 15 and 60 kilometers (9 and 37 miles) from the Polish border.
Belarus has a history of tensions with its NATO neighbors, including Poland and Lithuania. Minsk has previously been accused of using hybrid tactics against the two countries, including facilitating the arrival of migrants from the Middle East and Africa to its borders with the EU, which triggered a major migration crisis.
Belarus also allowed Russian forces to use its territory as a staging ground for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The exercises also come amid a buildup of military infrastructure along the Belarus-Ukraine border, leading Kyiv to warn that Moscow may be planning to draw its closest ally deeper into the full-scale war.

articles.title: Poland scrambles fighter jets, temporarily closes airports while Russian drones attack Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland scrambles fighter jets, temporarily closes airports while Russian drones attack Ukraine
Poland scrambled fighter jets and temporarily ceased operations of the airports in Lublin and Rzeszow on the morning of Sept. 16 as Russia launched drones against Ukraine, Polish authorities announced.
Around 7:00 a.m. local time, military aircraft took off and ground-based air defense and radar reconnaissance systems were readied in response to Russian drone attacks on Ukraine, Poland's Operational Command of the Armed Forces (DORSZ) announced on social media platform X.
This was a preventive measure to protect Polish airspace, particularly in the regions bordering Ukraine, DORSZ said. Shortly after 8:00 a.m. DORZS announced the operation had ended.
From 6:46 a.m. to 7:16 a.m., air raid alerts were issued in Ukraine's Volyn Oblast that borders Poland.
The Polish Air Navigation Services Agency (PANSA) announced that the airports in Lublin and Rzeszow temporarily suspended flights while the military operation was ongoing at 7:00 am. After 40 minutes, PANSA said the airports resumed activity.
The Government Security Center issued alerts for residents of Lublin and Podkarpackie regions for half an hour, Polish newspaper TVN24 reported.
Russia launched drones overnight at western Ukraine also on Sept. 13, striking a gas station near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing and a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train just 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Polish border.
Poland is treating Russian drone strikes near its border with Ukraine and the attack on a passenger train with the "utmost seriousness," Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said Sept. 13.
It was later reported that former U.K. Prime Minister Boris Johnson and other European officials were on the train in front of the one that was attacked and had passed through the border crossing shortly before.
Russian drone strikes "close to NATO territory" demonstrate Russian President Vladimir Putin’s "desperation," NATO General Secretary Mark Rutte said on Sept. 14.

articles.title: Kremlin Favored Russian General Awarded Medal for Fake City Capture Dies in Action
articles.body:
Russian Major General Anton Feliksovich Grunis, a senior officer actively profiled in Kremlin media as a brilliant tactician and battle winner in Ukraine, has died in a reported drone strike, Ukrainian official military and independent news sources reported on Tuesday.
Grunis, 46, was a native of the central Russian region of Tatarstan. His combat service included the 2nd Chechen War, the 2008 Russo-Georgian War, Russia’s invasion and takeover of Ukraine’s Crimea region in 2014, Russian military operations in Syria in 2015, and Russia’s second invasion of Ukraine begun in 2022.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Early reports of Grunis’ death surfaced in an encrypted Russian officer social channel called Surovovskoe Bratstvo on the messaging app Telegram. A death notice identified him as a graduate of the elite Kazan Suvorov Military Academy class of 1996, and comment by fellow students implied he died in combat.
Ukrainian information platforms led by the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) General Staff rebroadcast the death notice and confirmed it. The Independent reports and official Ukrainian sources did not state when or how Grunis died. Official Russian information platforms by Wednesday had not mentioned Grunis’ alleged death at all.
Drone footage published by Ukrainian army sources on Wednesday identified 427th Unmanned Systems Forces Brigade “Rarog” as responsible for killing Grunis in strikes near the village Kindrativka, Donetsk region, on Sept. 12. Imagery showed kamikaze drones boring in and detonating inside buildings geo-located to that place and substantial fires, however, that content showed no conclusive evidence Grunis or any other Russian service member had been hit.
‘Weeks’ Without Power: Partisans Claim Sabotage Hit Russian Missile Components Plant
Promotional footage released by Russia’s Ministry of Defense on Aug. 28 showed a live Grunis being awarded Russia’s highest medal for bravery “Hero of the Russian Federation” for success in battle, and stating to interviewers that he was honored and confident in Russian victory in Ukraine.
Grunis’ reported demise follows a rash of deaths in the Russian army’s upper ranks, including Lt. Gen. Damir Davydov’s assassination in a June 9 car bombing, Maj. Gen. Valery Plokhotnyuk’s death in an Aug. 1 Moscow restaurant bombing, and the killing of Lt. Gen. Sergey Milchakov , commander of Russia’s 51st Combined Arms Army, in a Ukrainian six-missile precision strike hitting his command post in the Donetsk sector on Aug. 26.
More senior officers, including generals, may have lost their lives in the restaurant bombing and the headquarters attack, because dozens had gathered at both places, Ukrainian military intelligence spokesmen said.
Grunis had been a high-profile officer in Russia thanks to his appearances in state-run media profiling him as a tough, frontline fighter with the call sign “The Terrible” (Russian : Грозный), and the man responsible for the capture of the major Ukrainian fortress city Kostiantynivka, in the east of the country.
Grunis’ command, the 4th Motor Rifle, in parallel content produced by Russia’s Defense Ministry and aired nationally, depicted the unit as an elite formation made up of Russia’s best soldiers, whose attacks with Grunis at the helm were unstoppable.
Grunis, in the June interview, praised his troops’ alleged skill in overcoming Ukrainian defenses with a hidden flanking movement through forests and swamps. The Ukrainian unit attacked by the Russians, the 156th Mechanized Infantry Brigade, was broken by infiltrating Russian foot soldiers supported by massed artillery and drone strikes that allowed a daring river crossing inside the city, Grunis claimed.
“All our units very quickly and successfully started operating on the left bank side of the city and exploited the success. As it worked out, we cut the city into pieces like a pie,” Grunis said. “Our great advantage was the Russian soldier. It is the dream of any commander, because no other army in the world has such soldiers as we do.”
Russian state television on July 3 aired video of Russian President Vladimir Putin receiving a formal report from his top general, Valery Gerasimov, that Kostiantynivka had fallen fully under the control of Russian forces thanks to Grunis’ 4th Brigade’s victory. Lower-ranking generals stood in the background were described in official media as a “command center near the front lines.”In fact, based on all other sources including official Ukrainian army statements, independent Ukrainian media, OSINT research groups, Western think tanks including the US-based Institute for the Study of War and six Ukrainian combat unit internal chat groups monitored by Kyiv Post and known to be deployed in the Kostiantynivka sector, Russian forces never came close to capturing the city and three months later it remains roughly under Ukrainian control.
The closest Russian forces came to pushing Ukrainian troops out of the city, per those sources, was with massed infiltration attacks in early July that sometimes isolated Ukrainian outposts in the center of the city for days before strike drones and assault infantry teams were able to locate the infiltrators and destroy them.Russian forces currently hold the southern districts of Kostiantynivka, Ukrainian forces’ fortifications in the north, and the center of the city is mostly a no-man’s-land out of the control of either side, those sources say. Reporting over the past week pointed to continuing Russian attempts to infiltrate foot soldiers into Konstantynivka’s Druzhivka suburb, with Ukrainian drone units operating in the vicinity claiming good results in attacking them.
Ukraine’s General Staff in a Wednesday situation update reported continuing Russian attacks in the Kostiantynivka sector with all assaults repelled. Unit information feeds for formations in that sector reported Ukrainian defenses within the city holding.
Ukrainian volunteer groups tracking Russian combat units and their members have, contrasting sharply with Kremlin messaging, long identified Grunis’ 4th Brigade as a troubled unit with soldiers complaining of officers’ extorting money in exchange for not being ordered on assault missions and soldiers’ unwilling to pay bribes or accept orders to make an assault, being locked in open-air pits until they change their mind. In a video, a man identifying himself as Sergei Moshchenko, a 4th Brigade rifleman, said that unit commanders ordered him and his mates to attack across open ground covered by Ukrainian drone swarms in an effective suicide mission, and that he and his buddies were new recruits with less than two weeks of training. During comments on Aug. 28, following the “Hero of the Russian Federation” awards ceremony, Grunis said he was “honored” to command “the best soldiers in the world.”
