articles.title: It’s official: The U.S. has weapons in space
articles.body:
In a first for the U.S. Space Force since its inception six years ago, the military branch has announced the deployment of weapons in space.
Speaking at the Air and Space Forces Association’s annual Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Monday, Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink declared that the U.S. has placed offensive technology into orbit, though he did not disclose any details about the weapons.
“We are increasing readiness against existing threats, and the United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action,” he said.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Although this is the first such acknowledgement from any global power, experts have long suspected space weapons are already a reality. In recent years, Russia has allegedly jammed communications satellites across Europe, and U.S. intelligence agencies have accused Russia of planning to put nuclear weapons in space. China, too, has demonstrated advanced capabilities for tracking and targeting satellites; these capabilities include a reusable space plane, similar to the U.S.’s X-37B, that could rendezvous with and capture adversarial spacecraft. Both Russia and China—as well as the U.S.—have a history of antisatellite missile tests and “cat and mouse” orbital encounters in which spacecraft maneuver to shadow or threaten others.
The U.S. deployment is a matter of necessity, Meink said in a press conference on Monday.
“Is there any question in the room, by anybody, about whether or not the Chinese or Russians have been developing these sorts of weapons?” he said. “For over a decade, we’ve been talking about the fact, and we have expressed concern, that the Chinese and Russians were developing weapons for space. We need to focus on making sure we can protect ourselves operating in that environment.”
According to Victoria Samson, chief director for space security and stability at the Secure World Foundation (SWF), the militarization is escalating rapidly in Earth orbit as more nations develop robust space programs. According to an SWF report co-authored by Samson from earlier this year, 13 countries have developed counterspace capabilities of some kind, including co-orbital satellites, which can disable or destroy other spacecraft, and space situational awareness satellites, which can track other objects in orbit.
“A lot of countries are saying, ‘We depend upon very heavily our space capabilities for national security reasons. They’re at risk; it’s a threatening environment. Therefore we need to build offensive capabilities that can threaten others,’” Samson told Scientific American before the Space Force announcement.
Despite their own well-documented military activity in space, both Russia and China responded to Monday’s announcement with statements warning against space militarization, with China opposing an “arms race” in the final frontier and Russia calling for the “complete demilitarization of space.” The current international framework for preventing space warfare is threadbare and filled with loopholes; signatories of the United Nations’ Outer Space Treaty of 1967 are merely obliged not to place weapons of mass destruction in orbit and to build no military bases and conduct no weapons testing on the moon or other planets.
Regardless of who is most culpable in the ongoing push for more and better offensive off-world capabilities, experts fear this announcement will further escalate the situation, raising the chances of space warfare that could prove ruinous for the entire world. John Barentine, an astronomer and formerly a policy expert at the International Dark-Sky Association (now DarkSky International), believes the militarization of space will ultimately prove “unwinnable” and will require a stabilizing doctrine similar to the Cold War’s nuclear threat of mutually assured destruction.
“I wonder if that’s not where we will end up with space militarization generally,” Barentine says, “where everybody rushes to acquire the technology, and we quickly realize that if war breaks out in space, it’s probably ‘game over’ for everybody.”
Other experts aren’t necessarily convinced this announcement will change much inhe ta galactic game of chicken. Among them is Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“With this disclosure, the U.S. is hoping that the knowledge of weapons on orbit may change behaviors. But without knowing exactly what these weapons could do and having a general sense of when the U.S. would decide to use them, it is hard to see China or Russia significantly altering their behaviors,” Swope says. “Deterrence requires convincing an adversary you will use a weapon, not just that you have one.”

articles.title: EXPLAINER – Human misuse or rogue machines? How advanced AI could threaten society
articles.body:
As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly powerful, warnings about the ways they could harm humans range from dangers already emerging today to fears of a future existential catastrophe.
Last week, Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon publicly resigned from the leading AI company, warning that developers were building systems that could ultimately destroy humanity.
“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Coxon posted on US social media platform X. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”
Soon after, leading AI executives backed calls to slow the development of increasingly powerful systems and strengthen safeguards, bringing concerns over the pace of AI development to the forefront of public debate.
"Recent warnings from AI researchers that advanced AI systems could pose a catastrophic risk to humanity should be taken seriously," Harin Sellahewa, dean of the Faculty of Computing, Law and Psychology at the University of Buckingham, told Anadolu.
While debate continues over whether highly advanced systems could themselves become a threat, Sellahewa said a more immediate concern is the possibility of people using increasingly powerful AI to cause large-scale harm.
"Advanced AI could amplify existing threats such as cyberattacks, misinformation, autonomous weapons, and other malicious activities," he said. “For this reason, the risks associated with both the technology itself and the ways humans may choose to use it warrant careful attention and appropriate safeguards."
Here are some of the ways AI could harm people:
AI is increasingly being incorporated into military systems, where it can analyze large amounts of battlefield information, identify objects, assist with targeting and help operate increasingly autonomous platforms.
Its use in warfare has raised concerns about what happens when machine-generated recommendations are wrong, insufficiently supervised or deliberately used to accelerate lethal decision-making.
Israel's use of AI-assisted systems in its war on Gaza has drawn particular scrutiny.
UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese, in her report From Economy of Occupation to Economy of Genocide, described how the Israeli military has used AI systems including Lavender and Gospel, as well as a system known as Where's Daddy?, to process information and generate or track potential targets.
The report also cited Project Nimbus, a $1.2 billion cloud-computing contract awarded by Israel to Google and Amazon in 2021, and said technology companies have played an expanding role in providing infrastructure and services used by Israel.
Albanese's report also said Palantir, whose work with Israel predates October 2023, expanded its cooperation with the Israeli government following the outbreak of the Gaza war.
Human Rights Watch warned in June that militaries were increasingly incorporating AI into life-and-death decisions, including targeting and weapons selection.
It cited reports that US forces used the AI-enabled Maven Smart System, integrated with Anthropic's Claude, during US-led strikes on Iran in 2026 to help identify priority targets and select munitions.
Anthropic said this month that it had also detected users in northern Yemen using Claude to support advanced weapons development.
The company did not identify the users as Houthis but said the activity originated in Houthi-controlled territory and included work on software for a guided rocket and a ballistic missile with a stated range of more than 2,000 kilometers (1,243 miles).
Cybersecurity is among the most immediate areas in which AI could contribute to physical as well as digital harm.
"In the near term, cybersecurity concerns, such as accelerated malware generation or automated vulnerability scanning, are the most plausible," Ruizhe Li, an assistant professor in the School of Computer Science at the University of Birmingham, told Anadolu.
Li said large language models are trained extensively on code repositories and software documentation, making them highly capable of understanding and generating computer code.
"Lowering the technical floor for sophisticated cyber exploits is therefore a tangible, near-term issue," he said.
AI can assist users in finding software vulnerabilities, writing malicious code, conducting reconnaissance and automating parts of cyber operations.
Anthropic said in its September threat report that it had disrupted attempts to misuse Claude in cyber operations, including activity involving phishing, malware and attempts to compromise computer systems.
An AI-assisted cyberattack targeting a hospital, electricity grid, water system, telecommunications provider or transport network could also disrupt services on which people's lives depend.
"What concerns me most are cyberattacks, attacks on critical infrastructure, and economic disruption," Sellahewa said.
"These are immediate and realistic risks because they can be amplified by human actors using advanced AI systems."
The same AI capabilities that can help scientists understand diseases, proteins and biological systems could potentially be misused to assist dangerous biological or chemical research.
Anthropic's September threat report described several cases in which users sought assistance for biological research that triggered the company's safeguards.
In one case, users sought assistance related to gain-of-function work involving the chikungunya virus, while others involved research into pathogens and toxins. Anthropic said it blocked the activity.
The concern is not that today's AI systems can independently create biological weapons, but that increasingly capable models could make specialized knowledge more accessible or accelerate work that previously required substantial expertise.
Li stressed the considerable gap between obtaining potentially dangerous information from an AI model and actually carrying out a biological or chemical attack.
"Catastrophic scenarios involving physical weapons, biological threats, or attacks on critical infrastructure require far more than generating text or code," he said.
"They demand complex coordination, specialized hardware, physical synthesis, and domain-specific infrastructure management. Current AI systems cannot autonomously navigate or execute these multifaceted physical pipelines."
AI can also cause harm by shaping what people see, hear and believe. It can already produce persuasive text, images, audio and video at scale and tailor messages to particular audiences.
Anthropic's September report documented AI-assisted influence operations involving fake accounts, websites and political content.
The risks can become particularly acute during wars, elections or public emergencies, when networks of AI-generated accounts could be used to spread false information, inflame tensions or encourage violence.
The riots that spread across parts of the UK following the killing of three girls in Southport in July 2024 offer an example of how AI-generated material can become part of a wider misinformation ecosystem.
False claims about the suspect's identity, religion and immigration status spread rapidly online after the attack and were amplified by far-right accounts before protests developed into riots in several cities.
Research by the London School of Economics found that one X account it examined posted dozens of AI-generated images promoting racist and Islamophobic narratives after the attack.
The researchers said 39 posts containing generative AI imagery attracted disproportionately high levels of engagement, with one receiving 11 million views.
Another category of concern involves direct interactions between AI chatbots and vulnerable users, with several lawsuits alleging that chatbot interactions contributed to fatalities including murders, overdoses and suicides.
In May 2026, the parents of 19-year-old Sam Nelson filed a wrongful-death lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging that ChatGPT gave him dangerous advice involving kratom, Xanax and alcohol before his accidental overdose death in 2025.
OpenAI has disputed the allegations and says ChatGPT is not a substitute for professional medical care.
Another lawsuit concerns an alleged murder-suicide in Connecticut.
The estate of 83-year-old Connecticut woman Suzanne Adams sued OpenAI and Microsoft, alleging that ChatGPT reinforced her son's paranoid delusions before he killed his mother and then himself.
A review published in The Lancet Psychiatry this year warned that large language models might contribute to the onset or exacerbation of psychotic symptoms, including by reinforcing delusional beliefs in vulnerable users.
- AI fraud and impersonation
AI can also make fraud more convincing and easier to carry out at scale.
In 2024, Hong Kong police said an employee at a multinational company was deceived into transferring about $25 million after fraudsters used deepfake technology to impersonate the company's chief financial officer and other employees during a video conference.
The employee reportedly joined a call with several people who appeared to be senior company officials. Police said the fraudsters had created deepfake versions of the executives and used them to convince the employee to make the transfers.
US authorities have also warned about criminals using AI-generated voices and messages to impersonate public officials and other trusted figures.
The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report said investment scams involving artificial intelligence resulted in more than $632 million in reported losses that year.
For Li, many of the most credible near-term dangers do not depend on AI becoming conscious, developing its own intentions or deciding independently to harm humans.
They come from people using increasingly capable systems to do things that were previously more difficult, expensive or technically demanding.
"Because large AI models ingest massive amounts of human text and code, they reflect both constructive and destructive patterns present online," said Li.
Without appropriate safeguards, Li said, such systems can lower the technical barriers facing malicious actors, including by helping generate deceptive content, phishing campaigns or malicious code.
"AI models do not act on their own desires, and their behaviors and outputs are steered directly by user input and system prompts,” he said.
"The core risk is human misuse, not rogue machines."

articles.title: Iran war cost hits $38bn, forecast to rise $3bn a month: CBO
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran war cost hits $38 billion, forecast to rise $3 billion a month: CBO
The six-month-old-and-counting US-Israeli war on Iran has cost $38 billion so far and that amount is projected to rise by $3 billion a month, Congress' nonpartisan bookkeeper reported on Tuesday, as the Trump administration searches for ways to end the conflict and reopen the vital Strait of Hormuz.
The war is expected to increase inflation by 0.5% in the first three months of 2027, according to the Congressional Budget Office accounting, which totaled expenses through 1 August.
The mounting costs have strained US munitions stockpiles and driven up energy prices, raising concerns about the country's ability to respond to other potential conflicts and adding pressure on an already stretched federal budget.
The cost was close to the $37.5 billion that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reported at a Senate hearing on 21 July.
The budget office said the majority of the costs stem from the rapid drawdown of munitions, estimating that it could take five years to replenish US stockpiles. Reuters reported in August that the US had used "virtually all" of its long-range precision missiles during the war.
The Department of Defense did not cooperate with congressional financial auditors, CBO reported.
White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly described President Donald Trump's attacks on Iran as "decisive action" to prevent Tehran from harming US personnel or interests. She said in a statement that the US military has "more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief’s strategic goals and beyond.”
Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell disputed the report's findings of munitions shortages and said, "We have everything required to strike at the time and place of the president’s choosing."
The cost inquiry was conducted at the request of the top Democrat on the US House of Representatives Budget Committee, Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania.
“Donald Trump’s disastrous war in Iran has already taken the lives of brave American servicemembers and left others wounded," Boyle said in a statement.
"Beyond that human toll, this nonpartisan CBO report makes clear that the war has also cost American taxpayers tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs."
The report did not include costs of recent strikes on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on US military installations in the region. It also did not factor in the borrowing expenses associated with financing the war, which could add tens of billions of dollars to the total cost.
Impact on US readiness
The CBO accounting found the war could have sprawling consequences for the US defense posture and the domestic economy.
The deficit in critical munitions, including missile interceptors, risks hampering the Pentagon's response in the event of another major conflict, such as potential hostilities involving China and Taiwan, CBO said.
At the July hearing in the Senate, Hegseth pleaded for nearly $90 billion in emergency funding to restock munitions supplies.
“Without these funds, we face critical shortfalls,” Hegseth said.
The Pentagon’s inspector general reported this week that Iran had damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings on US bases in the Middle East as well as aircraft including fighter jets, refueling planes and drones.
It put the war cost through June 19 at $33.4 billion, saying the amount included about $184 million in damages to US diplomatic facilities from Iranian strikes.
Energy shocks caused by attacks in the Strait of Hormuz—the narrow waterway through which roughly 20% of the world's oil traveled before the war—and on energy facilities in neighboring Gulf countries have sharply increased prices for consumers and global producers.
The rising cost of the war also threatens to weigh on deteriorating US fiscal health. The nation's total public debt surpassed $40 trillion in August.
Trump regularly contrasts the Iran war with the illegal US invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan that followed the 11 September 2001 attacks.
The eight-year US war in Iraq, which involved more than 100,000 ground troops at its peak, cost $2 trillion, Reuters reported. The two-decade-long US conflict in Afghanistan, which also involved more than 100,000 troops at its most intense, cost $2.3 trillion, according to Brown University's Costs of War project.

articles.title: Gaza war shines new light on Australia's most secretive spy base
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
'We want our land back and to stop the genocide': Gaza war shines new light on Australia's most secretive spy base
It was in mid-July when hundreds of activists gathered on the road leading up to the secretive military base in the heart of Australia.
They had arrived in the sleepy town of Alice Springs (Mparntwe) from across the country to demand the closure of a facility that has contributed to the historic dispossession of Indigenous Australians and is feared to be enabling the current displacement of Palestinians.
The US-led Pine Gap spy base has long been controversial in Australia. Since its establishment more than five decades ago, the facility has witnessed recurrent protests by activists opposed to the US military's presence and its occupation of land belonging to the Aboriginal Arrernte people.
But its presence has taken on a new significance since October 2023, when Israel began its genocidal assault on the Gaza Strip. Its activities remain shrouded in mystery, but it is believed to have played an important role in aiding the Israeli military in its destruction of the Palestinian enclave.
The three-day convergence, which took place on the 60th anniversary of the signing of the Pine Gap treaty, brought more than 600 pro-Palestine and anti-war activists, academics and politicians together with the Hayes family, the traditional custodians of the sacred land of Kuyunba.
The gathering culminated in hundreds marching to the base, chanting "From Arrernte to Gaza, Globalise the Intifada" and "Always was, always will be, Aboriginal land". At the gates, Arrernte Elder Felicity Hayes handed a letter to the local police chief asking for the land to be returned to its owners.
"We have every right to say we don't want this base here," Aunty Felicity told the inspector, before describing how her grandfather was taken advantage of to hand over the land without his consent.
Also among her requests was compensation for Palestinians in Gaza, where Israel has killed and injured almost a quarter of a million people since it began its assault in October 2023.
"Close the base because what it's doing is destroying other people's countries," she said. "We want our land back and to stop the genocide."
Nathalie Farah, a spokesperson for the convergence, said the protest was the largest at the facility since 1987. Farah, a Syrian-Palestinian activist in the Anti-Militarism Action Network, was among 100 people who had driven for four days from Melbourne to attend the gathering.
"We're very conscious of the fact that we can't stop what's happening in Palestine from Australia, but Australia plays a significant role in the system and if it can be stopped that system won't be as effective," she told The New Arab.
July's convergence was the third major protest to be held on the road to the base since October 2023, and it is unlikely to be the last.
Anti-war groups, trade unions and pro-Palestine activists are planning to hold rallies and events in cities and towns across the country on 20 September to protest the US military alliance, Israel's war on Gaza, and Australia's participation in AUKUS, the security partnership with the US and UK.
"What needs to happen is we need to build a proper anti-war movement here similar to what happened on this continent during the Vietnam war," Farah said.
From Australia to Israel
Australia's strategic position close to the Indo-Pacific has made the country an important location for US overseas military operations. In all, the US military controls 17 facilities in the country and has access to 75 more Australian-owned installations, according to recent research by the Nautilus Institute, an Australian think tank.
Northern Australia is of particular focus to the Pentagon. The US has invested hundreds of millions of dollars into building new military infrastructure in the area since 2024, making it the top overseas location for Air Force and Navy construction spending.
Pine Gap has attracted particular scrutiny because of the lack of oversight afforded to Australia's elected officials and its status as one of the most important American intelligence facilities outside the US.
The base, known officially as the Joint Defence Space Research Facility, is jointly operated by Australia's military and several American spy agencies, but Australian authorities are largely kept in the dark about the US's intelligence activities.
Classified US documents leaked by whistleblower Edward Snowden in 2013 revealed that the US National Security Agency (NSA) uses the facility to collect massive amounts of electronic signals and communication data. Intelligence is often used to identify military targets, including for drone strikes across the Middle East and Afghanistan.
Many suspect that Pine Gap has played a major role in the US's ongoing war on Iran, but the Australian government has remained tight-lipped.
The Snowden leaks also confirmed that Israel routinely receives intelligence from the NSA, with which it has eight intelligence-sharing agreements.
In 2023, investigative news site Declassified Australia published testimony from a former NSA employee who said that the base collects intelligence on Gaza.
"We know that signals intelligence data, captured by Pine Gap-controlled Orion satellites, has been historically made available to Israel," said Professor Richard Tanter, a senior research associate at the Nautilus Institute who is widely regarded as the country's leading expert on the base.
"Unless the Australian direct and indirect military relationship to Israeli activities in the Gaza Strip are closely reviewed by the Inspector General of Intelligence and Security, it is not possible for the Australian government to assure the parliament and the Australian public that Australia is not complicit in acts of genocide," he added.
"The base's intelligence-sharing with the Israeli military has been one of the key ways that Australia has failed to uphold its obligations under the Genocide Convention," Jorgan Doyle, a spokesperson for the convergence, told The New Arab.
Doyle is an organiser for Mparntwe for Falastin, a local pro-Palestine group set up after 7 October 2023 that has staged fortnightly rallies on the road to the base and held frequent events and vigils in the town.
He described the Australian government's approach to the US military relationship as "don't ask, don't tell", which he says is particularly problematic given expectations that the country will soon host nuclear-capable American bombers.
The Tindal air base, located 1,000 kilometres north of Pine Gap, is being expanded by the US to host up to six B-52 bombers, which are expected to arrive by the end of the year.
Political backing
The campaign has attracted support from the Australian Greens, whose senators have called on the government to rethink its military alliance with Washington. Lawmakers in the left-wing party have been staunch critics of the Israeli military's actions in Gaza and have called for cutting trade ties with Israel and sanctions on ministers in the government.
The Greens, while still a minor party, are currently polling in fourth with around 15-16% of the vote and hold 10 seats in the 72-seat Senate.
"We don't want to be a part of the United States's forever wars," Senator David Shoebridge told The New Arab.
The New South Wales senator attended the convergence and plans to submit the Hayes family's letter for a debate in parliament later this year. Among the family's demands are the closure of the base, the return of the land to its traditional owners, and the payment of compensation to the dispossessed Arrernte people and families in Gaza.
"First Nations owners of the land on which Pine Gap sits have never given consent to the US presence, they don’t want their land contributing to US wars and the killing we can all see in places like Iran, Palestine and Venezuela," Shoebridge said.
"Australians are watching as the US becomes an agent of chaos, causing instability and violence in the world… For the first time since the Iraq war, we have a mass movement of people in Australia taking a clear stance against US war and our government's role in them."
The campaign against Pine Gap comes as polls show falling support for the US among the broader public amid the chaos of the Trump administration.
Successive surveys have shown that, while the military relationship remains popular, Australian voters are increasingly supportive of a more independent foreign policy and are less willing to trust the alliance with the US.
A poll by the Lowy Institute in June found that just 21% of Australians have confidence in the US president. Meanwhile, the University of Sydney's United States Studies Centre found that a third of the public believe that the second Trump administration has been very bad for Australia, while almost four in 10 see the US as mostly harmful for Asia.
Doyle, of Mparntwe for Falastin, said the convergence happened at a "really interesting geopolitical moment" amid shifting public opinion.
"We increasingly hear ordinary Australians becoming uneasy about the US alliance and Australia's place in the world," he said.

articles.title: US Charges Five in Russian Intelligence Network Over Violent Plots in America and Europe
articles.body:

US Charges Five in Russian Intelligence Network Over Violent Plots in America and Europe
The US Department of Justice has charged five alleged members of a Russian intelligence network accused of recruiting operatives for terrorist attacks in Europe and plotting to assassinate a Russian dissident in the United States, US Attorney General Todd Blanche announced.
According to the US Department of Justice, the five defendants allegedly operated as part of a global network working on behalf of Russian intelligence services since at least 2024. The network specialized in organizing contract killings and acts of terrorism, with its activities targeting Russian dissidents and defectors as well as countries supporting Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“It is our job to stop America’s adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil. And that’s precisely what we are doing thanks to the work of the FBI and our Justice Department prosecutors,” Blanche said.
According to ABC News on September 16, the case, filed in the Southern District of New York, centers in part on an alleged plot to assassinate a prominent Russian dissident whom the defendants believed was in Washington, DC.
US investigators identified 63-year-old former Russian intelligence colonel Yuri Khrameev and his son, 27-year-old FSB officer Kirill Khrameev, as alleged leaders of the network. Investigators said its leadership also included 35-year-old Cuban national Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, who resides in Russia.
Two other defendants, 35-year-old Cuban national Yaidel Delgado Suarez and 22-year-old Venezuelan national Angel Eduardo Castro, helped identify and recruit potential operatives in the United States.
“These defendants allegedly operated as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin,” Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg said.
According to investigators, the network recruited a US resident during the summer of 2026 to conduct surveillance and help arrange the killing of a prominent Russian dissident. The alleged recruiters offered between $1,000 and $1,500 for surveillance and $40,000 for the killing.
The indictment also describes an earlier effort in Lithuania, where the network allegedly recruited a US citizen in 2025 to surveil a person whom the Russian operatives described as spreading damaging information about Russia. Yuri Khrameev later allegedly offered the recruit $25,000 to kill the Russian dissident using either an incendiary device or a knife.
After the individual refused, Khrameyev proposed what he described as simpler assignments involving arson attacks against food warehouses or electrical substations. Investigators said he identified potential targets as countries supporting Ukraine and promised substantial payments.
The alleged network’s activities extended beyond assassination plots. Investigators said Durruthy coordinated preparations for an attack in Prague, Czechia, in June 2024 and another planned attack in Lithuania in September of that year.
“The Russian-led network charged in today’s indictment is brazen, aggressive, and far-reaching, and the charges levied against the defendants should send a clear message: no matter where you are, and no matter who you work for, we will investigate and prosecute you for your crimes,” US Attorney for the Southern District of New York Jay Clayton MacDonald said.
All five defendants remain at large. They have been charged with conspiracy to finance terrorism, which carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. Three of the defendants also face conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire charges, punishable by up to 10 years in prison.
The charges come amid broader efforts by European countries to counter suspected Russian covert operations and hybrid threats. Germany and Ukraine have agreed to strengthen security cooperation in response to such threats, with Ukrainian intelligence and law enforcement specialists set to share their experience in countering drones, sabotage, espionage, and cyberattacks.

articles.title: Ukraine has 'successfully tested' new interceptor against Russian jet-powered drones, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Ukraine has 'successfully tested' new interceptor against Russian jet-powered drones, Zelensky says
Ukraine has "successfully" trialed another interceptor drone designed to target Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, President Volodymyr Zelenskysaid Sept. 15 following a briefing by Ukrainian Armed Forces Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi.
As Russia expands its arsenal of Shahed-type jet-powered drones, including the Geran-3, Geran-4 and Geran-5, and the cruise missile-like Banderol loitering munition, Ukraine is facing mounting difficulties intercepting the weapons during prolonged attacks, with Kyiv and the surrounding region frequently targeted.
"A 'shahed' was hit successfully, but some aspects of controlling the interceptor still need to be refined. The work continues – it will take some more time," Zelensky wrote on X.
The jet-powered drones can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour (nearly 370 miles per hour), making them more difficult to intercept than earlier, piston-powered Shahed variants. Their use also increased sharply this summer, rising roughly fivefold in July compared with June, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said Aug. 31.
Russia launched nearly 800 jet-powered drones toward Ukraine over four days in late August, according to Zelensky.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said Aug. 29 that Ukraine had field-tested four potential interceptors against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, without specifying which companies were developing them or how far along the projects were.
Anatolii Hrapchynskyi, deputy director of an electronic warfare company and a reserve Air Force officer, told the Kyiv Independent that the use of jet-powered drones was to be expected as Russian forces had been seeking ways to overwhelm Ukraine's anti-aircraft defenses.
Hrapchynskyi said that at the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Russian troops had only expensive long-range weapons at their disposal, which could be launched from strategic aircraft, submarines, or the coast.
Russia most recently used jet-powered drones in a Sept. 15 attack on Kyiv that killed at least one person and injured 12 others. The daytime strikes damaged residential buildings, a data center, and two gas stations in the capital.

US exposes five Russian agents who planned killings and terrorist attacks

Quote from Blanche: "It is our job to stop America's adversaries from unleashing violence and terror on American soil. And that's precisely what we are doing thanks to the work of the FBI and our Justice Department prosecutors."
Details: Blanche said that the suspects had worked for Russian intelligence and planned a series of assassinations around the world.
In particular, the group was preparing an attack on a "Russian dissident" whom they believed was in Washington.
The case is being heard in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York.
Update: According to the unsealed indictment, the Russian agents have been working for Russian intelligence services since at least 2024 and specialised in organising contract killings and terrorist attacks.
"The RIS Network is one arm of the Russian Federation's apparatus to carry out external attacks, including murder, and has focused on Russian dissidents and defectors and, most recently, on nations perceived as allies of Ukraine," the department said.
Investigators consider the leaders of the intelligence network to be 63-year-old former Russian intelligence colonel Yuri Khramyeev and his 27-year-old son, Federal Security Service (FSB) officer Kirill Khramyeev. The leadership also included 35-year-old Cuban national Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, who lives in Russia.
The other two defendants, 35-year-old Cuban national Yaidel Delgado Suarez and 22-year-old Venezuelan national Angel Eduardo Castro, were tasked with finding and recruiting potential operatives in the US.
"These defendants allegedly operated as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin," said John Eisenberg, US Assistant Attorney General for National Security.
According to investigators, in summer 2026, Russian agents recruited a US resident to conduct surveillance and arrange the murder of a prominent Russian dissident, offering US$1,000 to US$1,500 for surveillance and US$40,000 for the killing. After the recruit refused to carry out the assassination personally, his handlers asked whether he could find other people to do the job.
In addition, last year the network recruited a US citizen in Lithuania to conduct surveillance on a person whom the Russians called a "bad guy" who was "telling lies" about Russia. Later, Colonel Yuri Khramyeev offered the American US$25,000 to kill the Russian dissident by "throwing a bottle of gasoline" or "sticking a knife" in him.
After the refusal, Khramyeev senior offered the American a "simpler job", involving setting fire to food warehouses or throwing incendiary mixtures at electrical substations. The Russian intelligence officer stressed that their targets were "all the countries that are helping Ukraine" and promised "serious money".
The investigation also established that in June 2024, Durruthy, a Cuban national, coordinated preparations for an attack in the Czech capital Prague, and in September of the same year for another terrorist attack in Lithuania.
"The Russian-led network charged in today's indictment is brazen, aggressive, and far-reaching, and the charges levied against the defendants should send a clear message: no matter where you are, and no matter who you work for, we will investigate and prosecute you for your crimes," said Jamie McDonald, US Attorney for the Southern District of New York.
All five suspects are currently at large. The defendants are charged with conspiracy to finance terrorism, which carries a sentence of up to 20 years in prison, while three of them are also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire, which carries a sentence of up to 10 years in prison.
Background:
- Western countries have repeatedly documented the activity of Russian assassins on their territory. The best-known incidents include the poisoning of former FSB officer Alexander Litvinenko in London in 2006 as well as the attempted assassination in 2018 of former Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation (GRU) agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia in Salisbury in the UK using the "Novichok" chemical agent.
- In August 2019, Russian officer Vadim Krasikov shot and killed former Chechen field commander Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in Berlin.
- The US Department of Justice regularly initiates criminal cases against Russian nationals over cybercrime, espionage and sanctions evasion. However, the exposure of plans to physically eliminate dissidents directly on US soil indicates a significant escalation in the activities of Russian intelligence services.

articles.title: Ukraine war drives European demand for bigger, cheaper missile arsenals
articles.body:
Ukraine war drives European demand for bigger, cheaper missile arsenals
- European militaries are shifting to cheaper, mass-producible missiles and interceptors due to high consumption rates in conflicts like Ukraine, highlighting the limits of small inventories of expensive weapons.
- Startups and established companies are developing low-cost missile systems to complement advanced weapons, aiming to reduce interception costs from millions to around €1-2 million.
- The main challenge for Europe is scaling industrial production capacity to rapidly produce and replenish missile stocks required for modern large-scale conflicts.
AI generated
BRUSSELS - European militaries are increasingly exploring cheaper missiles and interceptors after conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East exposed the limits of small inventories of high-end weapons.
Along Europe’s eastern flank, Russia’s daily drone and missile attacks on Ukraine have highlighted a lesson often overlooked in peacetime procurement planning: modern conflicts can consume weapons faster than many countries can replace them.
“If you think you have enough cruise missiles in your inventory, you probably don’t,” said Douglas Barrie of the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
Analysts say Europe’s defence sector spent years focused on small production runs of sophisticated weapons rather than wartime-scale manufacturing, leaving governments now racing to seek lower-cost systems that can be fielded in greater numbers alongside advanced weapons from companies such as Lockheed Martin, MBDA and Rheinmetall.
Industry executives say the challenge is no longer missile design but building the manufacturing capacity needed to sustain a modern conflict.
“Big wars are fought with numbers, not wonder weapons,” said Stockholm International Peace Research Institute researcher Markus Schiller.
A new generation of defence startups says it can help meet the demand by developing cheaper missiles and interceptors designed for large-scale production.
The Netherlands in June ordered 700 Ruta Block 2 cruise missiles from European startup Destinus for Ukraine in a €250 million (S$367 million) deal, while Britain’s Ministry of Defence awarded initial Skyhammer interceptor contracts to Cambridge Aerospace.
“Given how the battlefield has evolved since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, developing low-cost but effective weapons systems is important,” the Estonian Defence Forces told Reuters.
The arithmetic of modern war
Ukraine has already built a layered response, downing many of the thousands of long-range drones Russia launches each month with mounted machine guns, interceptor drones and electronic warfare to preserve more advanced interceptors for higher-end threats.
Steven Barrett, chief executive of Cambridge Aerospace, said Russia could launch up to 900 Shahed-type drones in a single night. Attempting to defeat them with traditional interceptors, as the US has at times done in the Middle East, “would cost billions of dollars per night... which is just impossible for any of our allies to sustain,” he said.
Andreas Bappert, chief technology officer of missile company Frankenburg, said future systems must reduce the cost of a successful interception from as much as €20 million to around €1 million to €2 million.
Ukrainian startup Fire Point says it aims to build a ballistic-missile interceptor for less than €1 million, roughly one-quarter to one-sixth the cost of a US-made Patriot air-defence interceptor.
Lockheed Martin in 2026 unveiled a lower-cost Patriot missile. But even at less than half the cost of a Patriot PAC-3, it would remain above startup targets and is not expected to enter production until 2028.
Unlike the PAC-3, which is designed to defeat ballistic missiles and advanced aircraft, many of the emerging low-cost systems are focused primarily on drones, cruise missiles or other lower-end threats. Industry executives and analysts say they are intended to complement rather than replace high-end air-defence systems.
Can Europe build enough?
Investors are increasingly backing emerging missile makers as they seek to scale production. Cambridge Aerospace raised US$300 million (S$382 million) in August to expand production, while Destinus is pursuing additional funding ahead of a planned IPO.
“The challenge for Europe is not that the technology does not exist,” Destinus founder Mikhail Kokorich told Reuters. “The bigger challenge is industrial capacity, or the ability to produce, qualify and replenish systems on the scale required by modern conflicts.”
Cambridge Aerospace is investing heavily to secure rocket motors and other critical components while incorporating commercial technologies such as automotive radar chips.
Fire Point uses a network of manufacturing partners, while Destinus has plugged into Rheinmetall’s industrial base through a joint venture announced earlier in 2026.
Cambridge Aerospace aims to produce 2,500 interceptors a month by the end of the first quarter of 2027, while Frankenburg is targeting output of up to 100 missiles a day and 1,500 missiles in 2026.
Industry executives say scaling production depends not only on funding but also on securing components, obtaining approvals and expanding manufacturing processes.
Fire Point hopes to demonstrate a successful ballistic-missile interception by mid-2027, compressing what Chief Executive Iryna Terekh said would otherwise be a decades-long process into a few years.
Frankenburg chief executive Kusti Salm said manufacturing capacity itself could become a deterrent if adversaries concluded Europe could rapidly replace missiles consumed in combat.
“If the enemy knows that we can produce en masse ... the equation tells him, I’m not going to reach my objectives,” he told Reuters. REUTERS

Ukraine Strikes Russian Su-24 at Saky, Threatening Crimea-Based Aviation Operations
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Su-24 combat aircraft at the Saky airfield in temporarily occupied Crimea on September 15 and overnight into September 16, the country's General Staff reported.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine announced the operation on its official Telegram channel on September 16.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the statement, Ukrainian defense units struck “a number of important military targets of the Russian aggressor” during the attacks.
Beyond the Saky strike, the General Staff listed additional targets hit across temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories:
- A storage, preparation, and launch site for Russian strike drones near the city of Donetsk;
- drone control points in Staromlynivka and Pokrovsk in the Donetsk region, and in Pokrovske in the Zaporizhzhia region;
- an ammunition depot in Dovzhansk in the Luhansk region;
- fuel and lubricant storage bases in Rovenky in the Luhansk region and Berdiansk in the Zaporizhzhia region;
- "Grenadier" technical reconnaissance posts in Suvorove and Rysove in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The Su-24 is a Soviet-designed supersonic tactical strike aircraft built for all-weather, low-altitude attack missions and recognizable by its variable-sweep wings and side-by-side cockpit.
The upgraded Su-24M variant carries guided missiles, bombs, and rockets across multiple hardpoints and remains a mainstay of Russian tactical aviation. Damage to such an aircraft further thins the pool of strike planes Moscow operates from temporarily occupied Crimea.
The upgraded Su-24M variant remains in Russian service and can carry guided missiles, bombs, and rockets across multiple hardpoints.
The General Staff said operations against Russian military targets would continue.
“Work on key military targets of the enemy continues,” the statement said.
The Saky airfield has repeatedly featured in Ukraine's campaign against Russian military aviation in temporarily occupied Crimea.
On August 22, Ukrainian forces destroyed a Su-24M aircraft and four pieces of airfield equipment there, alongside strikes on drone-control relay stations in Russia's Bryansk region.

Poland Scrambles Jets as Russia Attacks Western Ukraine With Jet-Powered Drones
Poland scrambled fighter jets overnight on September 15 in response to renewed Russian attacks on western Ukraine involving jet-powered strike drones, Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command reported.
At around 4 a.m., the Operational Command said Polish and allied aircraft had been deployed as Russian jet-powered drones carried out strikes against targets in Ukraine. Ground-based air defense and radar systems were also placed on heightened readiness.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The measures were taken as a precaution to protect Polish airspace and “aimed at securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions.”
At around 6:30 a.m., the Operational Command announced that the potential threat had passed and that the forces and systems activated during the alert were returning to standard operational status.
“No violations of Polish airspace were recorded,” the Operational Command said.
The heightened readiness in Poland came as NATO responded to another aerial incident elsewhere on its eastern flank. Earlier the same night, NATO aircraft intercepted and destroyed an unidentified drone that entered Lithuanian airspace, with preliminary information indicating that it had arrived from Belarus, according to Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT.
The drone crossed into Lithuania shortly after midnight, triggering air alerts in several areas. About 30 minutes later, NATO fighter jets operating from the Šiauliai Air Base intercepted and shot down the aircraft over the Kaunas region.
Lithuania’s military said Italian fighter jets carried out the interception. The drone’s wreckage was subsequently found in a rural area, where police cordoned off and secured the site.
The incidents follow another recent airspace breach involving a NATO member. On September 8, Romania deployed two F-18 fighter jets after military radar detected an aerial object entering Romanian airspace at around 4:47 p.m., roughly 18 kilometers north of Roman.
The detection prompted air raid warnings in several nearby communities. Shortly beforehand, at approximately 4:20 p.m., neighboring Moldova reported that a drone, preliminarily identified as a Shahed, had entered its territory.

articles.title: Caught between the US and China, can Switzerland stay neutral in the AI race?
articles.body:
Caught between the US and China, can Switzerland stay neutral in the AI race?
The debate over neutrality is particularly heated in Switzerland ahead of a vote on the issue on September 27. But what does it mean to be neutral in a world where artificial intelligence, cloud services and digital infrastructure increasingly depend on the United States and China?
For more than two centuries, Swiss neutrality has defined Switzerland’s position in armed conflicts. On September 27, Swiss voters will decide whether to enshrine a more restrictive interpretation of neutrality in the Constitution limiting the country’s ability to impose sanctions on belligerent states outside those decided by the United Nations Security Council.
Whatever the outcome of the vote, the question of how to remain neutral in a world in which artificial intelligence (AI) and other strategically important technologies are controlled by two rival powers – the United States and China – is as pressing as ever. This issue is particularly sensitive for Switzerland, which depends heavily on technologies developed by both countries.
“If you are in the middle, you get caught in the crossfire,” says Jean-Marc Rickli, head of global and emerging risks at the Geneva Centre for Security Policy.
Driven by economic competition and geopolitical tensions, the US and China are accelerating the development of increasingly powerful AI systems, even “at the expense of security,” Rickli says. The rise of advanced, autonomous agentic AI models is an example.
“With agents, you have new entities that are potentially able to develop and carry out their own plan, including staging their own attack without human intervention, in order to reach their assigned goal. And this is something completely new,” Rickli says. In this environment, he believes the danger of mistakes or escalation is becoming more tangible.
Maxime Stauffer, co-founder and CEO of the Simon Institute for Longterm Governance, a Geneva-based think tank, believes that advances in frontier AI are changing the cyberspace threat landscape.
“Day to day, various states and non-state actors launch cyberattacks on each other. That’s known and almost routine. But there used to be an equilibrium between offense and defence capabilities, which AI is now disrupting,” he says.
The growing US-China rivalry over AI has even prompted comparisons with a new “Cold War”, although the analogy remains contestedExternal link.
Despite the calls, neither Washington nor BeijingExternal link appears willing to slow down the AI race. “We’re leading China in AI (…) and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins,” US President Donald Trump said recentlyExternal link. China, for its part, has dismissed calls to slow down the development of AI, calling them “fearmongering” and part of a “Cold War playbook”.
Both countries use access to their technology, sanctions and industrial dependencies for geopolitical leverage. In this context, remaining equidistant between Washington and Beijing is becoming “increasingly difficult,” Rickli says, “because you have to choose a side, in order to avoid potential sanctions”.
According to the Swiss State Secretariat for Security Policy (SEPOS), US and Chinese companies’ growing influence over countries’ economic and military capabilities and the conduct of warfare is “jeopardising strategic stability”.
>>Here is everything you need to know about the upcoming neutrality on September 27:
More
How the neutrality initiative could affect Swiss policy
The law of neutrality also applies in cyberspace
Does this mean Swiss neutrality has become irrelevant in the digital world?
From the perspective of international law, the answer is no. “The fact that the law of neutrality was codified before the advent of cyberspace and artificial intelligence does not mean that it does not apply in these areas,” says Marco Roscini, professor of international law at the University of Westminster in London and an expert on neutrality and armed conflict.
Roscini explains that the general rules governing armed conflict – reflected in the United Nations Charter, the Hague Conventions and the Geneva Conventions and Protocols – remain binding regardless of the technology employed. This was established by the International Court of Justice in a 1996 advisory opinionExternal link. What matters, therefore, is how technologies are used as means or methods of warfare.
For Switzerland, this entails both legal protection and obligations. In the event of a war between China and the United States, for example, Bern would have to take feasible measures to stop either side from using cyber infrastructure on Swiss territory to conduct hostilities against the other.
“Cyberspace is not an abstraction. Clouds, cables, satellites, data centres, servers, computers and the people who use them still have a physical location,” Roscini says.
SEPOS notes, however, that the application of international legal norms to new technologies – including in cyberspace and outer space – is in some respects unclear, or that governments prevent such norms from becoming established.
Sovereignty rather than technological neutrality
Much of Switzerland’s technological dilemma, according to the experts interviewed, does not actually concern the law of neutrality. Dependence on US and Chinese software, digital services or AI systems is primarily a question of sovereignty and strategic autonomy.
The law of neutrality, Roscini points out, primarily applies to the state, not private companies. Switzerland has long taken advantage of the absence of general trade restrictions to do business while remaining neutral. During the Second World War, for example, Swiss companies continued trading with belligerent states, especially Nazi Germany, despite the country’s neutral status.
For to Eugenio Benincasa, a senior cybersecurity researcher at the Center for Security Studies of the Swiss federal technology institute ETH Zurich, a similar strategy characterises Switzerland’s relations with China and the United States today. Switzerland maintains substantial economic relations with both, benefiting from each without fully aligning itself with either side. But this technological dependence, while not in itself compromising Swiss neutrality, “limits the country’s room for manoeuvre,” Benincasa says.
The initiative being put to a vote on September 27 could further limit Switzerland’s room for manoeuvre. By severely restricting Bern’s ability to impose sanctions on belligerent states, it could have repercussions for the country’s reputation and economic interests, according to the Swiss governmentExternal link. Switzerland would no longer be able to join numerous sanctions against countries at war, with the exception of those decided by the United Nations Security Council, where the United States, China and Russia each have veto power.
>>Here’s how the Swiss arms industry has capitalised on neutrality:
More
Arms trade: Swiss neutrality as business strategy
To strengthen its digital sovereignty, Benincasa believes Switzerland should seek to reduce dependencies in the most sensitive sectors, such as critical infrastructure, public administration, defence, intelligence and healthcare. And where Swiss alternatives are unavailable, the country should at least rely on European technologies.
In practice, Switzerland already makes different calculations depending on the technology and the supplier, Benincasa says. In the case of Palantir, a US company specialising in data analytics and security technologies, several Swiss public institutions, including the armed forces, have decided against using its software, partly because of concerns over sovereignty and national security. In other sectors, by contrast, Chinese technologies such as Huawei’s cost-competitive telecommunications infrastructure can be particularly difficult to replace.
“Asymmetric assessments are made based on what the two countries can offer,” Benincasa says. “Talking about complete technological independence is a utopia.”
The diplomacy card
There is, however, one area in which Swiss neutrality could be an asset: diplomacy, not least thanks to the presence of intergovernmental organisations based in Geneva. Historically, neutrality has enabled neutral states to help prevent conflicts from escalating and offer good offices, mediation and humanitarian assistance.
Maxime Stauffer of the Simon Institute in Geneva says Switzerland’s status as a neutral state still helps create space for dialogues on AI amid rapid technological developments and geopolitical tensions.
Stauffer mentions possible areas for such dialogue, including maintaining communication channels to reduce the risk of unintended escalation involving autonomous systems and setting boundaries on AI use against critical infrastructure.
The Swiss foreign ministry has not confirmed the existence of any official Swiss mediation between the US and China on artificial intelligence. But if Switzerland’s current approach to neutrality can genuinely help it mitigate the risks of cyberwar between the two technological powers, it may be less outdated than some might think.

Disgruntled troops leak PHOTOS of extensive damage to US bases from Iranian strikes
US troops have leaked new images to CBS News capturing widespread destruction at American military bases across the Middle East from Iran’s missile and drone attacks.
The servicemen who provided the photos chose to stay anonymous because of harsh media restrictions in the US military, the outlet said in an article on Tuesday.
“This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public,” one of the soldiers stationed in the region said.
The service member complained about insufficient air defenses at the US facilities, saying “we’re standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face.”
The Iranian munitions that are getting through are “not ‘squirters’” as US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth called them after six American troops were killed in a strike on a US military tactical operations center at the Port of Shuaiba in Kuwait in early March, the soldier stressed. “We’re not defending these bases. We’re just watching them get destroyed.”
🚨🇺🇸 🇮🇷 BREAKING: Troops leaked photos of their wrecked bases to CBS, saying they're "standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face"
Active service members sent the images anonymously. 
One soldier's words: "We're not defending these bases. We're just watching… pic.twitter.com/zvxEyxB8wm
CBS News said that the photos it had received showed a $300 million US E-3 Sentry radar plane destroyed by a direct hit at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia as well as damaged buildings and burnt-out vehicles at Camp Buehring and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait.
Earlier this week, the US War Department’s inspector general issued a report, saying that the American forces have suffered $3.7 billion in equipment losses, including almost 60 aircraft, during the war against Iran, which started in late February with a US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic. 
American bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan were hit, with hundreds of buildings and structures being damaged or destroyed, according to the inspector.
Last week, the acting secretary of the US Navy, Hung Cao, told the Epoch Times that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain,” referring to the attacks on the American military facilities in the Gulf country.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi responded to the acknowledgment in a post on X, saying that “our powerful Armed Forces did indeed ‘blow the hell out of the 5th Fleet HQ in Bahrain,’ as well as other bases supporting US aggression.”
In early September, Iranian Parliament speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned that further aggressive actions by the US will be met with “faster, heavier and more painful” retaliation by Tehran.
“The Americans have surely understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end and our recent strikes against aggressor bases were only a start,” Ghalibaf said.

articles.title: Von der Leyen pitches European Security Council in response to Trump and Putin
articles.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday said she would propose a new security forum for EU and like-minded leaders in response to escalating Russian attacks and fraying transatlantic relations.
It's part of a broader rethink of security policy that includes a more robust response to hybrid attacks attributed to Russia and a greater effort to build up Europe's own defense capabilities — although in conjunction with NATO.
“For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent with partners like Ukraine, the U.K., Norway, Canada and others involved,” she said in her annual State of the European Union address.
Advertisement
“This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play — this is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality,” she said. "The urgency is clear."
The proposal underscores growing fears that Europe is struggling to deal with rapidly proliferating airspace violations, cyberattacks and sabotage attempts amid tensions linked to the Kremlin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with NATO wary of escalating its response amid fears of setting off a war with Russia.
The transatlantic alliance has also been strained by growing tensions between U.S. President Donald Trump and European allies and Canada. Trump threatened to annex Greenland earlier this year, is recalibrating U.S. forces in Europe and has threatened Canadian sovereignty, fueling doubts over Washington’s commitment to the transatlantic alliance.
“This is a Europe that stands up for each other,” von der Leyen said, “like when we stood up for Greenland when threatened.”
Various versions of a European Security Council have been floated since the 1980s but none have gained traction. The idea resurfaced after an EU split over the 2003 Iraq war and was given fresh impetus in 2017 by former EU executive chief Jean-Claude Juncker and French President Emmanuel Macron, but failed because of U.K. reluctance.
Green MEP Sergey Lagodinsky resuscitated a formal proposal for a UN-style security council this year, arguing for an intergovernmental treaty that would bring together Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Poland and the U.K. alongside two rotating seats for smaller countries to speed decision-making in crises.
Advertisement
EU capitals have generally been skeptical of handing over their jealously guarded powers on defense to new institutions. The pitch also risks a clash with NATO, which has repeatedly warned Brussels against duplicating the alliance's security mission.
The Commission chief also said she would propose an EU emergency security protocol modeled on NATO’s Article 4 urgent consultation procedure to respond to hybrid attacks that fall below the threshold of armed aggression but still threaten national security.
“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook,” she said. “When triggered by one member state, all member states would convene to coordinate a European response — to deter further escalation and to mitigate the impact.”
To bolster Europe’s efforts to take charge of its own defense, von der Leyen also floated a new scheme for building European strategic military capabilities such as air-to-air refueling and air and missile defense — areas where the continent still relies heavily on U.S. technology.
“I can announce a new European Instrument for strategic enablers — fully aligned with NATO,” she said. “These systems are essential, and we need more of them. Only together does Europe have the scale to deliver them.”
Manfred Weber, who leads the center-right European People’s Party group in the European Parliament, echoed that call and warned of the danger posed by Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Advertisement
“The threat is clear — Putin won’t stop,” he said, speaking after von der Leyen's address. “Our answer is unity … joint command structures, European drones, European satellites so closely connected that no one can ever undo this cooperation.”
Weber said such joint action should reduce the fragmentation of European defense efforts, which leads to waste and duplication among member countries. The goal is not to create "27 bonsai armies," he said.

The strike was conducted jointly by the 429th Achilles Brigade and the 43rd Separate Artillery Brigade using a RAM-2X drone, which hit the radar approximately 175 kilometers from the line of contact.

articles.title: North Korea says US prepares to use WMDs against it
articles.body:
PYONGYANG, September 16. /TASS/. The United States and South Korea under the pretext of responding to the threat of weapons of mass destruction are preparing to use nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons against North Korea, the North Korean Defense Ministry said in a statement released by the Central News Agency of Korea (KCNA).
"This is an outright declaration of confrontation aimed at using nuclear, chemical, and biological weapons against our state in the event of a war on the Korean Peninsula and at accelerating preparations for a real war," it said.
The reason for its publication was a September 10 meeting of the US-South Korea Commission on Response to Weapons of Mass Destruction. According to Pyongyang, the parties agreed to develop information exchange, enhance joint response capabilities, and intensify relevant exercises.
The Defense Ministry also noted that scenarios for responding to the use of weapons of mass destruction were being practiced during the joint US-South Korea Freedom Shield exercises. Pyongyang believes this increases the risk of such weapons use in the region.
The statement says that the United States is developing military·biological activities at facilities in various regions of the world and is allocating funds for the development, testing, and use of chemical and biological weapons. Pyongyang described Washington’s assertion about the threat posed by other states’ weapons of mass destruction as a pretext for its own developments in this area.
The Defense Ministry warned that in response to such actions, the law on the policy regarding state nuclear armed forces, which allows the use of nuclear weapons may be invoked. The actions of the United States and South Korea will be taken into account when assessing the security threats facing the people’s republic, and the armed forces will continue to monitor the military activity of Washington and its allies.
The 2022 law allows the use of nuclear weapons in the event of an attack on the country’s leadership and the nuclear forces control system, as well as in the event of a threat to use nuclear or other weapons of mass destruction against North Korea. It also allows the use of nuclear forces in the event of a threat to strike important strategic facilities and provides for the automatic delivery of a nuclear strike according to a pre·approved plan if the nuclear forces control system is threatened as a result of an attack.
