articles.title: Iran: Architects of crimes against humanity to suppress protests must face international justice to deter further massacres
articles.body:
- New report finds Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their bloody suppression of the 2022 Woman Life Freedom uprising
- In-depth investigation exposes chain of command responsible for implementing state policy of lethal force to crush protests and identifies 87 officials who should be investigated for crimes against humanity
- Iranian authorities disproportionately targeted Kurdish and Baluchi communities with lethal repression and subjected them to the crime against humanity of persecution
- UN General Assembly should create an international criminal justice mechanism to tackle impunity for repeated mass protest killings culminating in January 2026 protest massacres
- Report released amid armed hostilities since unlawful US and Israeli attacks, underscoring the need for enduring ceasefire and accountability for violations of the UN Charter and international humanitarian law
In a landmark new report marking the fourth anniversary of the start of the Woman Life Freedom uprising, Amnesty International warns that those responsible for crimes against humanity committed to brutally crush nationwide protests in 2022 continue to control Iran’s deadly state machinery of repression today.  
The report, Architects of Atrocities: State Machinery Orchestrating Crimes Against Humanity in Iran’s 2022 Woman Life Freedom Uprising –more than 1,000 pages long – details how Iranian authorities committed the crimes against humanity of murder, torture, enforced disappearance, imprisonment, rape and persecution on political, gender, ethnic and religious grounds in order to crush the uprising. It also documents deadly protest repression operations and command structures, identifying 87 officials who should be criminally investigated for crimes against humanity.
Amnesty International is calling for an international criminal justice mechanism to be established urgently by the UN General Assembly to ensure Iranian authorities responsible for crimes against humanity are held to account and to deter further atrocities such as the large-scale protest massacres committed on 8-9 January 2026.
In light of the ongoing hostilities following unlawful attacks by the USA and Israel on Iran, Amnesty International also reiterates its call for an enduring ceasefire and independent investigations into attacks committed during the conflict. The organization calls for the UN to address accountability for violations of the UN Charter and of international humanitarian law, including possible war crimes.
“The extensive evidence gathered and analysed in our report leaves no doubt: Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity to crush the 2022 Woman Life Freedom uprising. They waged a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population demanding dignity, human rights and fundamental political change, pursuant to a state policy of using lethal force to obliterate dissent,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
Our report unveils how crimes against humanity in Iran are sustained by an architecture of impunity built into the country’s constitutional, legislative, political and judicial frameworks.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General
“Our report also unveils how crimes against humanity in Iran are sustained by an architecture of impunity built into the country’s constitutional, legislative, political and judicial frameworks. The horrifying result has been intensifying cycles of mass protest killings, culminating in the massacres of thousands of protesters within just 48 hours on 8-9 January 2026. The UN General Assembly must end the unconscionable normalization of mass protest killings in Iran and create an international criminal justice mechanism aimed at prosecuting those most implicated in crimes against humanity.
“This report is being published at a time when people in Iran are also facing the devastating consequences of unlawful attacks by the USA and Israel. Amnesty International unequivocally opposes violations of international law by all parties and rejects any attempt to instrumentalize the suffering of victims of human rights violations in Iran to justify unlawful attacks that inflict further civilian harm.
“For years, Iranian people have faced brutal repression, persecution and impunity at the hands of their own authorities. Today, many are also bearing the human cost of unlawful military action carried out by the USA and Israel. A principled response requires rejecting both impunity for crimes against humanity and unlawful use of force. The international community must pursue people-centred diplomatic strategies that place civilian protection, atrocity prevention, justice and accountability at their core. After more than six months of air strikes that have killed and injured civilians, damaged the environment, and caused significant destruction of civilian infrastructure, an enduring ceasefire is urgently needed alongside independent investigations and action by the UN General Assembly to address accountability for violations of the UN Charter and of international humanitarian law and possible war crimes committed by all parties to the conflict.”
Amnesty International’s report, released four years after the death in custody of Zhina Mahsa Amini at the hands of the “morality” police sparked nationwide protests, documents how the Iranian authorities mobilized security forces armed with military-grade firearms and shotguns loaded with metal pellets and issued orders that facilitated the unlawful killing of hundreds of protesters and bystanders, including dozens of children. The crimes against humanity also included the arbitrary arrest, enforced disappearance, torture or other ill-treatment of thousands of men, women and children as well as persecution of bereaved relatives.
Alongside the report, Amnesty International is also publishing Lives Cut Brutally Short: Victims of Crimes Against Humanity During Iran’s 2022 Woman Life Freedom Uprising, a document recording the deaths of 377 protesters and bystanders, 56 of them children, based on information and evidence gathered as part of the organization’s investigation into nationwide patterns of killings by the security forces. The document includes victims’ photographs and images of their grave sites where available.
In addition to calling on the UN General Assembly to create an international justice mechanism given the political deadlock at the UN Security Council, the gravity and scale of crimes committed, and high risk of recurrence, Amnesty International also urges states to call on the UN Security Council to refer the situation in Iran to the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court.
The organization also urges prosecution authorities around the world to initiate investigations, under universal or other forms of extraterritorial jurisdiction, against Iranian officials allegedly responsible for crimes against humanity, including the officials named in this report, and, where sufficient evidence exists, to issue arrest warrants.
Amnesty International’s years of research for this report involved interviews with 270 people, including protesters, former detainees, relatives of those killed or detained, eyewitnesses, lawyers, human rights defenders, journalists and medical workers. The organization also analysed over 2,000 videos and extensive documentary evidence, including official statements, leaked official documents, prosecution orders, court verdicts and forensic records.
Amnesty International wrote to Iran’s Supreme Leader and senior security officials to share its findings and notify the 87 officials identified in the report. At the time of publication, it has received no response.
A nationwide attack carried out pursuant to state policy
Amnesty International’s investigations into crimes against humanity committed to crush the 2022 Woman Life Freedom uprising revealed that two main security forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) and the Police Command of the Islamic Republic of Iran (known by its Persian acronym, FARAJA), led lethal protest dispersals, implementing the state policy devised through the Supreme National Security Council, State Security Council and provincial and county security councils.
FARAJA and IRGC agents repeatedly fired into crowds, using military-grade assault rifles, handguns and shotguns loaded with metal pellets. In addition to firing into crowds, they chased fleeing protesters and bystanders, closing in on unarmed victims who posed no threat to the security forces or others and fatally shooting them at close range.
Among the FARAJA branches involved were the Prevention Police, including its Assistance Cohorts, and the Special Cohorts. The IRGC branches involved included the operational divisions, the provincial Security Cohorts and various Basij battalions, such as the Imam Ali Battalions and the Beit Al-Moghaddas Battalions. These IRGC branches operated under the relevant IRGC provincial corps, overseen in turn by a regional IRGC headquarters.
Official statements and leaked documents analysed in the report reveal the state policy as reflected in strategy meetings, binding orders, deployment plans, allocations of money and weapons, and instructions for a “firm and severe” response. One leaked order instructed forces to “respond mercilessly and go as far as causing death”.
Witnesses repeatedly described streets resembling battlefields as a result of relentless gunfire by the security forces. Mahshid, who protested in Mahabad, West Azerbaijan province, told Amnesty International: “I had never seen such scenes before… The situation was very frightening and felt like a war zone. The security forces just kept shooting.”
Most of the 377 protesters and bystanders, whose deaths Amnesty International recorded, were killed by security forces during protest dispersals between September and December 2022. Others died in custody, after release from custody or in suspicious circumstances suggesting state responsibility.
Consistent with long-standing patterns of denial and cover-up, the authorities have acknowledged only 202 deaths and falsely attributed most to non-state actors, “rioters” or “armed terrorists”, despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary. Far from acting to stop crimes as evidence mounted, senior officials repeatedly praised security forces and instructed the continuation of operations.
Total of 87 officials identified for criminal investigation
Based on detailed documentation of the security forces involved and in-depth analysis of their command structures, Amnesty International has identified 87 Iranian officials who should be criminally investigated for crimes against humanity.
The list, while not exhaustive, extends from the highest levels of Iran’s security apparatus to officials operating at provincial and county level.
The list of 87 individuals comprises 62 security force commanders – including 33 commanders from the IRGC and 27 commanders from FARAJA – and 25 Ministry of Interior officials including provincial and county governors. Among them are 10 national-level officials and 77 officials at regional, provincial and county levels holding responsibilities related to the 17 counties in Kurdistan, Kermanshah and West Azerbaijan provinces on which Amnesty International conducted in-depth investigations.
Among those identified is the late Supreme Leader and commander-in-chief of all armed forces, Ali Khamenei; and the late head of the General Staff of the Armed Forces, Mohammad Bagheri, both of whom were killed in February 2026 in air strikes carried out during the US-Israeli military attack against the Islamic Republic of Iran. Amnesty International also names the then minister of interior, Ahmad Vahidi, who has since become the General Commander of the IRGC, and the then deputy minister of interior for police and security, Majid Mir Ahmadi.
This investigation exposes the layers of command and coordination behind the Iranian authorities’ deadly protest crackdowns.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International
“This investigation exposes the layers of command and coordination behind the Iranian authorities’ deadly protest crackdowns. The agents on the streets operated within a hierarchical and coordinated chain of command linking them to officials who directed, enabled, facilitated and supported crimes committed on a massive scale,” said Agnès Callamard.
“The officials named remain beyond the reach of justice in Iran. Most remain in positions from which they can unleash further deadly repression while some even climbed the chain of command after the crimes against humanity in 2022. The cost of continued impunity has been devastating. It is beyond time to establish an international criminal justice mechanism for Iran before another protest massacre.”
Devastating toll on Kurdish and Baluchi communities
Protesters from Iran’s persecuted Baluchi and Kurdish communities suffered a devastating share of the lethal repression, accounting for 62% of the total number of recorded victims while they constitute 5% and 10-15% of the country’s population, respectively.
Amnesty International recorded the unlawful killing of 106 Baluchi protesters and bystanders, including 20 children, by security forces in Sistan and Baluchistan province (33% of recorded victims). On 30 September 2022 alone, 87 were unlawfully killed as security forces opened fire following Friday prayers in Zahedan – a crackdown widely known as “Bloody Friday”.
The organization also documented the circumstances surrounding the unlawful killing of 95 Kurdish protesters and bystanders, including 13 children, in the context of protest dispersals or in militarized areas near protests that were ongoing or had recently occurred across 17 counties in Kurdistan, Kermanshah and West Azerbaijan provinces (29% of recorded victims). Most were fatally shot; others were fatally beaten, struck by tear gas canisters or deliberately run over by security force vehicles.
Iman, an eyewitness in Sanandaj, Kurdistan province, said: “The agents would shoot anyone in their sight, not caring if they were women, children, passersby or protesters.”
Amnesty International found that in the provinces of Kermanshah, Kurdistan and West Azerbaijan, security forces consistently deployed designated marksman rifles, assault rifles, sub-machine guns and heavy machine guns mounted on top of pickup trucks.
Amnesty International has concluded that acts of murder and torture were committed against Kurdish and Baluchi protesters with discriminatory intent on political and ethnic grounds, and that that the elements of the crime against humanity of persecution are met for these targeted groups.
Impunity by design
In Iran, impunity for crimes under international law and other serious human rights violations is systemic and intentional.
Iran’s constitution places the justice system under the direct control of the Supreme Leader, who is not only the commander-in-chief of the security forces, but also appoints the head of the judiciary, who in turn appoints senior judges and prosecutors. Cases involving serious human rights violations by members of the security forces are handled by military prosecution offices and courts, where judges and prosecutors can themselves come from the security forces and routinely rely on accounts from the very security bodies implicated in crimes.
Iran’s Law on the Use of Firearms by Armed Forces in Necessary Incidents allows firearms to be used to disperse protests, in blatant disregard of international law, which permits the use of firearms only as a last resort to counter an imminent threat of death or serious injury. The law also generally exempts state agents from civil and criminal liability.
“Survivors and victims’ families in Iran have been trapped in a system where the very institutions meant to deliver justice are controlled by authorities with blood on their hands. Families who seek truth and justice are persecuted,” said Agnès Callamard.
Directing calls for accountability to Iranian judicial authorities complicit in crimes against humanity is detached from reality. The international community must advance international pathways to justice now.
Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International
“Directing calls for accountability to Iranian judicial authorities complicit in crimes against humanity is detached from reality. The international community must advance international pathways to justice now. The UN General Assembly must confront the crisis of impunity that exposes people in Iran to recurring and escalating mass protest killings.”
Background
Amnesty International is launching this report while people in Iran are at risk of crimes under international law on two fronts. On one front, they are exposed to violations of international humanitarian law since the USA and Israel unlawfully attacked Iran in violation of the UN Charter on 28 February 2026.
On the other, they risk further crimes against humanity in the context of protest crackdowns. Iranian authorities have used the cover of “wartime conditions” to intensify internal repression, further militarizing public spaces, openly threatening to carry out mass killings against protesters and dissidents, and escalating politically motivated arbitrary executions.
Iran has been gripped by successive waves of anti-establishment protests since December 2017, as protesters have repeatedly taken to the streets demanding human rights, dignity, freedom, the end of the Islamic Republic system and transition to a new rights-respecting system of governance. Amnesty International’s extensive research into the authorities’ response to successive waves of protests in December 2017-January 2018, November 2019, September-December 2022 and January 2026 reveals a recurrent pattern of mass unlawful killings, torture, enforced disappearance and other crimes under international law.

articles.title: Watchdog: War with Iran has depleted US weapons reserves
articles.body:
The US Department of Defense Inspector General has reported that the war with Iran has caused a munitions shortage and a “bottleneck” in replenishing stockpiles—contradicting statements by US President Donald Trump, who regularly denies the existence of supply issues, the BBC reports.
Trump has previously claimed that US munitions reserves are virtually unlimited and that anyone saying otherwise is spreading fake news. However, the independent watchdog reported that between February and June, the US expended munitions worth over 22 billion dollars, resulting in a shortage of strategic equipment. When asked about the watchdog’s report, the White House responded that there is more than enough ammunition.
The report provides the first independent insight into typically classified information regarding US weapons stockpiles.
Previous estimates had already painted a grim picture. During the conflict, US forces expended large quantities of ammunition for long-range systems, as well as vast numbers of missiles and air-defense munitions, to repel Iranian strikes. In late July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) concluded that stockpiles of ammunition for certain missile interception systems—such as Patriot and THAAD—had been significantly depleted, with inventories in some cases cut by as much as half.
The Inspector General’s report does not disclose the exact quantity of remaining weaponry;
however, it indicates that equipment is running low and reveals bottlenecks in the ammunition replenishment supply chain. The report adds that the Department of Defense is working to accelerate procurement processes and production capacity to address the ammunition shortage.
The White House has rejected the watchdog’s assessment; on the 15th of September, spokesperson Anna Kelly stated that the United States possesses more than enough ammunition to achieve all its strategic objectives—and then some. Trump and other US administration officials have also sought to portray reports of weapons shortages as a betrayal of the country.
In a post on X on the 4th of August, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth dismissed reports of weapons shortages as false. Meanwhile, in a lengthy post on Truth Social on the 3rd of September, Trump emphasized that the US holds virtually unlimited stockpiles of weapons and continues to build up its inventory to prepare for any contingency. When the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran, Trump stated that the conflict would be over within a few weeks. In September, he said that the war in Iran would end after the midterm elections scheduled for the 3rd of November.
Polls show that the war in Iran is highly unpopular among Americans. A survey conducted in early September indicates that only 23% of Americans (and just half of Republican voters) believe the US is in a better position regarding Iran than it was at the start of the war.
Read also: Gulf states cancel meeting with Iran; Houthis attack Saudi Arabia

articles.title: US disavows need to invite France, UK to strategic stability dialogue — Lavrov
articles.body:
YEKATERINBURG, September 16. /TASS/. Washington firmly rejects the need to engage Paris and London in strategic stability talks in the event of expanding the dialogue, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said, addressing the International Festival of Youth.
Today, the United States "insists that strategic stability be discussed at trilateral talks with China," Russia’s top diplomat said. "We, for one, tell the Americans that, unlike us and China, which are not bound by any allied obligations in the military field, the United States alongside France and Britain, which too possess nuclear weapons, does have such obligations," he continued.
"Therefore, if we ever consider expanding the circle of participants in the dialogue, we should first of all pay attention to that troika, something that the Americans resolutely oppose," Lavrov explained.

articles.title: U.S. Army rebuilds long-range missile stocks drained by the war on Iran
articles.body:
- The U.S. Army awarded Lockheed Martin $1.21 billion to develop Precision Strike Missile Increment 2, adding a seeker that lets the long-range missile strike moving land and maritime targets.
- The contract follows reports that the Army's PrSM stockpile was heavily drawn down during Operation Epic Fury, the recent U.S. military campaign against Iran.
The U.S. Army has awarded Lockheed Martin $1.21 billion to keep developing an upgraded version of its long-range strike missile, work that comes as the Army tries to rebuild a stockpile it drained fighting Iran earlier this year.
A Department of War announcement said the contract funds early operational capability work on the Precision Strike Missile Increment 2. It is structured as an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity award, so the Army will issue individual task orders against that ceiling rather than lock in a fixed number of missiles now. Army Contracting Command at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, is managing the deal, listed as contract number W31P4Q-26-D-A001. One company bid on the work, and Lockheed won it. The estimated completion date is Sept. 13, 2031.
The Precision Strike Missile, known as PrSM, is a ground-launched, long-range strike weapon the Army built to replace the aging Army Tactical Missile System. It fires from the M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System and the M270 tracked launcher, and two PrSM rounds fit in a launch pod that used to hold a single ATACMS. Each missile costs just under $3.5 million, according to the Army’s own budget documents. The baseline version, Increment 1, reached Army units in December 2023 and hits fixed points on land out to roughly 500 km (310 miles) using GPS and inertial navigation. It has no ability to track something that moves. Australia is also buying into the program: Canberra has signed on as a full development partner and in April selected PrSM, paired with HIMARS, as its own land-based maritime strike system.
Increment 2 is meant to give the missile the moving-target ability the baseline version lacks. Lockheed is integrating a new multi-mode seeker, developed under a separate Army effort called the Land-Based Anti-Ship Missile program, that lets the missile identify and strike a target in motion, whether that is a mobile air defense radar or a ship underway. The Army’s Combat Capabilities Development Command Aviation and Missile Center built the guidance package before handing it to the PrSM program office for integration. The new seeker adds this capability on top of the missile’s existing land-attack role rather than replacing it.
Lockheed flew the first Increment 2 test missile with the new seeker in March 2026, sending it about 350 km (217 miles) from a HIMARS launcher. The missile deployed protective covers over the seeker at launch and gathered performance data engineers are still reviewing. The program remains in a technology-maturation phase, with a preliminary design review underway, and Lockheed has additional flight tests planned later this year.
“With Increment 2, PrSM delivers the long-range capability the Army asked for to defeat moving land and maritime threats,” said Carolyn Orzechowski, vice president of precision fires launchers and missiles at Lockheed Martin.
The urgency behind this contract traces back to a war the Army did not expect to fight this hard with these missiles. The Defence Blog reported in March 2026 that U.S. Central Command had confirmed PrSM’s first combat use, during Operation Epic Fury, the American military campaign against Iran. The Army fired the missile at Iranian coastal radar sites, air defense positions and other targets, and the campaign consumed the stockpile far faster than planners expected. Reuters, citing two people familiar with the matter, reported the Army expended “virtually all” of its ATACMS and PrSM inventory during the operation. A separate analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies put the loss at roughly 45 percent of the Army’s Precision Strike Missile stockpile in the war’s first seven weeks alone, figures Pentagon sources told CNN were consistent with classified internal data. The Army has never disclosed how many PrSMs it had before the war, and it still has not said how many remain. Independent estimates of replacement timelines run from three to five years to fully rebuild the stockpile.
This contract does not, by itself, answer that shortage. It funds Increment 2 development rather than a specific quantity of new missiles, and the Army has separately been placing production orders for the baseline Increment 1 to refill the pipeline Reuters and CNN described. The IDIQ structure gives the Army flexibility to keep ordering PrSM rounds as Lockheed’s production capacity allows, rather than commit to one large batch now.

articles.title: GFEAI 2026: science minister warns AI potential to become an invisible dictatorship
articles.body:
GFEAI 2026: science minister warns AI potential to become an invisible dictatorship
TEHRAN – Science, Research and Technology Minister Hossein Simaei-Sarraf has warned that the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in data analysis could pave the way for a shift from data control to human control, potentially giving rise to what he described as “an invisible dictatorship.”
Simaei-Sarraf made the remarks while addressing the 4th Global Forum on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (GFEAI 2026), held in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, from September 14 to 17, IRNA reported.
 
 Leading an Iranian delegation to the forum, the minister stressed the need to give serious consideration to the ethical implications of emerging technologies.
“Technology is not neutral, and artificial intelligence does not operate fairly on its own. Sometimes, algorithms destroy more than they build, and platforms become sources of harm rather than development,” he said.
Enhanced transparency and oversight of governments and those in power are essential. However, when the surveillance is directed at ordinary citizens, tracking their behavior, relationships, and intentions, it can turn into an invisible dictatorship, he added.
Referring to the ethical responsibility of AI platforms and developers, the science minister said, “Today, data is being used in ways that violate human rights and even lead to the death of children, thereby raising a significant question: do AI platforms accept the responsibility for how their technologies are used?”
Numerous chatbots refuse to answer questions about suicide—and rightly so—yet AI can be employed to identify and precisely target human beings with missiles, as the elementary school in Minab was targeted by US missiles, killing 168 students while they were studying.
According to Simaei-Sarraf, inequality is another fundamental challenge of the AI era. Unequal knowledge and capabilities have always created disparities. AI can widen the gap more than any other technology. Hence, the ethical framework should not be merely limited to preventing harm, but to ensuring equal access.
Developing countries should have the opportunity to develop their own AI systems tailored to their languages and cultures, and international organizations are ethically responsible to help these nations realize this goal. Technology must serve humanity, and AI should enhance human freedom, not limit it, he further noted.
In response to a question about the country’s most important measure to strengthen Iran’s capacity in responsible AI, Simaei-Sarraf said if this question was raised before June 2025, he would have definitely said targeted and sustainable investment in water and energy sectors, followed by strengthening collaborations within Iran’s AI ecosystem.
Regarding the shift in regional priorities, the science minister went on to say that “today, I think the removal of coercive measures and the establishment of peace in the region are the top priorities for Iran as well as the whole region. These sanctions are unethical, and establishing security and peace is a moral imperative.”
The Global Forum serves as a key platform to advance the implementation of the Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence across all Member States of UNESCO. It supports the exchange of knowledge and experiences across regions in the development of AI policies, regulatory frameworks, and institutional capacities, to foster inclusive and sustainable social and economic development while safeguarding human rights and fundamental freedoms.
Launched in 2022, the Global Forum was previously hosted by the Czech Republic, Slovenia, and Thailand, with co-funding support from the European Union since 2024.
The 2026 edition of Global Forum aims to create an engaging environment with high-level ethical reflection, bridging discussions on governance with technological innovation. The science minister is scheduled to attend specialized meetings, panel discussions, and hold meetings with representatives of other countries.
Co-hosted by UNESCO and Saudi Arabia, represented by the Saudi Data and AI Authority and the International Centre for AI Research and Ethics, the event has brought together global leaders, policymakers, experts, and stakeholders to strengthen dialogue and promote practical and sustainable approaches to the ethics and governance of AI.
 
 MT/MG

articles.title: 12 takeaways from von der Leyen’s State of the Union
articles.body:
Ursula von der Leyen used her State of the Union speech to unveil a raft of proposals aimed at making Europe better prepared for a world of threats — from sweltering summers to hybrid warfare, migrant crises and social media.
What the Commission president chose to talk about in Strasbourg — and, just as importantly, what she left unsaid — will help define the rest of her term and the political legacy she leaves behind.
Here are the 12 biggest takeaways.
Advertisement
1. Canada could become the EU’s first “associate member”
Speaking directly to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was sitting in the Parliament hemicycle, von der Leyen proposed an ambitious, far-reaching new alliance spanning tech, defense, energy, critical minerals, AI, the Arctic and more.
In a message that could have been addressed directly to U.S. President Donald Trump, von der Leyen said: “This is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength.”
While it remains to be seen whether EU member countries are on board with so-called associate membership — a model, it should be noted, that does not currently exist — the proposal is a striking signal of how badly Brussels wants to deepen ties with Ottawa.
2. Europe might finally get a security council
The idea of a European security executive body has been floated in various forms for years, but has taken on fresh urgency against the backdrop of Trump undermining the transatlantic security relationship and Russia’s war against Ukraine spilling over into the bloc.
Von der Leyen injected new life into the discussion by calling to create a European Security Council, saying it would bring together the EU and like-minded countries, including the United Kingdom, Canada, Ukraine and Norway (notably, there was no mention of the U.S.) to discuss and manage threats.
Advertisement
It would go hand-in-hand with a new “Emergency Security Protocol,” which EU countries could trigger in response to threats short of an actual attack or invasion. “In other words, a mechanism to flank NATO’s Article 4,” she said.
3. EU wants to work together on AI, but not with the U.S. or China
The Commission president is inviting the major AI labs to Brussels to discuss efforts to “pace the frontier” of AI development.
“AI comes with a balance of possibilities and risks,” she said. “Without addressing these risks, we will never be able to unlock AI’s possibilities.”
A woman uses her laptop at a metro station in Kyiv on Nov. 27, 2025. | Sergei Gapon/AFP via Getty Images
Von der Leyen called for cooperation with the United Kingdom, Canada “and others” on AI but did not mention the U.S. or China — the two countries leading the global AI race.
Von der Leyen said the remaining funds would be used for a new program involving joint projects with Ukrainian defense companies.
Advertisement
The announcement potentially turns an administrative problem — member countries such as Italy not taking up all the cheap loans available to them — into a way to integrate Ukraine's battlefield expertise and defense industry with Europe's.
5. Climate policy is becoming more about survival
Von der Leyen's climate message was notably focused on preparing for the worst rather than new emissions-cutting measures.
She defended the EU's existing climate targets but devoted much of her attention to dealing with the consequences of a hotter Europe, including a forthcoming European Heatwave Plan, a European Water Initiative and a Climate Insurance Alliance.
She said there can be “no repeat of this summer,” which was Europe’s hottest ever, causing its forests to burn and its rivers to dry up.
6. Von der Leyen wants to stop “gold-plating”
The Commission president wants EU countries to agree on a new “pact against gold-plating” — the practice of adding national requirements when implementing EU legislation.
“We are doing our best at the European level to cut red tape. But now I think it is time for the member states to step up,” she said.
Advertisement
While von der Leyen called for the overhaul of the single market to be completed by the end of 2027, she otherwise glossed over simplification and competitiveness in her speech.
7. Admitting defeat on Israel
Von der Leyen acknowledged the “deep suffering” in Gaza and condemned “unchecked settler violence” in the West Bank, while saying Europe must keep the two-state solution alive.
But she also openly acknowledged the EU's inability to agree on some of the measures she promised last year, with member countries unable to agree on action.
Destroyed buildings are seen in Gaza on June 10, 2026. | Ahmed Al Arini/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images
The failure to secure majorities for sanctions against Israeli settlers and ministers, she said, was “painful for many Europeans.”
“When Europe is divided, it cannot change the course of events,” she added.
8. Surprisingly little to say about finance
For a Commission that has spent much of the past year talking about making Europe a more attractive place to invest and scale up, financial policy was largely absent from the address.
Advertisement
Von der Leyen's main new financial announcement was a Banking Package focused on simplification and tackling fragmentation — a proposal the Commission had already announced in July.
There was little new on the broader ambition to turn Europe into a major investment hub.
“To be very clear, our budget is about our future. And any modern budget needs new own resources,” she said, referring to the term for EU taxes.
The Commission’s proposal to generate over €60 billion through new levies has been met with resistance in national capitals.
10. China got an ominous mention
One of the questions looming over the speech was how hard von der Leyen would go in on China.
Advertisement
On Wednesday, she slammed the EU's trade deficit with Beijing — “one billion a day. It has reached a tipping point,” she said — and highlighted “dangerous dependencies” on China for critical raw materials.
But on trade, she stopped short of calling for any dramatic measures — something she did in her 2023 speech — when she launched an anti-subsidy investigation into electric vehicles. “We will use all the tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationship,” she said this year, in an apparent reference to the EU's still-under-construction diversification instrument, but did not go further.
11. Getting tough on migration
In the wake of the Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen called for a European Emergency Response Framework, which would give EU countries in similar scenarios “time-limited and strictly defined flexibility in standard procedures.” Translation: returning migrants faster without worrying about granting asylum.
She also wants the bloc to strengthen Frontex, its border agency, but did not mention raising staff numbers, as she has called for previously.
12. Banning kids from social media
Von der Leyen took aim at social media, which she said was stealing childhoods, and vowed tougher action to protect kids online, including keeping some minors off popular platforms like TikTok and Instagram.
“No social media under the age of 13. No personal account under the age of 15,” she said, adding platforms would also have to introduce “safe design” for under-18s.

articles.title: US Charges 5 In Russian Intelligence Sabotage And Assassination Plot
articles.body:
Russian intelligence agencies oversaw a series of surveillance and assassination plots targeting dissidents in the United States and Europe, US authorities charged, adding to a growing number of warnings about Russian spy operations in the West.
The allegations, detailed in a new federal indictment, were also the latest warning from Western officials detailing how Russia increasingly uses people not trained as professional spies --- sometimes unwittingly -- to carry out operations.
Among the five people charged in the indictment unveiled late on September 15: a father and son linked to Russia's Federal Security Service: Kirill Khrameyev, identified as a colonel in the agency, known as the FSB; his father, Yury, identified as a retired FSB officer.
Three others -- two Cuban men named Oemis Durruthy and Yaidel Suarez and a Venezuelan man Angel Castro -- were also charged. Durruthy lives in Russia, the US Justice Department said in a statement. The whereabouts of the two others are unclear.
According to the indictment, as recently as this summer, Castro, who had been living in Brooklyn, New York, was hired to surveil a prominent Russian dissident who was living in Washington, D.C.
The Russian dissident is not identified in the court filings.
The person was sent to two addresses and given “explicit instructions on how to conduct surveillance,” authorities said. In exchange, the person was promised $1,000 and $1,500 to carry out the surveillance.
The person then allegedly sent photographs to one of the FSB officers, who then later offered $40,000 to the person to “eliminate” or “disappear” the dissident.
After the person declined the offer, the FSB officers allegedly sought out others in the United States to carry out the murder plot.
In another incident detailed in the indictment, an American man living in Lithuania traveled to Estonia, to the border with Russia on June 25, 2025.
There, he met Khrameyev who allegedly offered to pay the man an unspecified amount to return to Vilnius and take photographs of an address where a “bad guy” who was “telling lies about Russia" lived.
The person was paid $200 for the surveillance. The person was then put in touch with Khrameyev’s father, Yury, who allegedly offered him $25,000 to kill the person because he was "spreading dirt about my country" and "telling the media and the common people that the Russians are the aggressors."
Khrameyev also explained how the killing could take place, including "throwing a bottle of gasoline" or "sticking a knife" in the person," according to the court filing.
After the person declined, Yury Khrameyev allegedly proposed he could set fire to a warehouse or electrical substation for an unspecified amount of money.
Khrameyev allegedly wrote to the man, saying he was offering "serious money for serious work," and he was interested in targeting pro-Ukrainian countries, according to the indictment.
The group was also accused of a plot to set fire to buses in the Czech Republic. Durruthy, US authorities said, enlisted a Colombian man, who allegedly tried to burn public buses in the capital, Prague.
After the man's arrest, the Czech prime minister said the plot was "very likely" organized by Russian authorities.
The FSB had no immediate comment on the charges.
Neither Yury nor Kirill Khrameyev could be reached for comment either.
Photographs posted by Kirill Khrameyev to the Russian social media platform VK show him posing at a St. Petersburg academy graduation ceremony, alongside his father.
The indictment includes extensive quoted material taken from chat messages, as well as photographs, that were exchanged between the Khrameyevs and their contacts.
It does not specify how the material was gathered, but in past years, US authorities have used search warrants to access cloud-based storage services -- for example Apple's iCloud, or Google Drive -- to obtain backed-up files, including things like WhatsApp chat logs.
Other plots have been uncovered by authorities accessing Google Translate files stored online, according to the investigative website The Insider.

articles.title: EU chief calls for NATO-like EU security mechanism
articles.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen gestures as she delivers a speech during her annual State of the Union address at a plenary session of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, eastern France on September 16, 2026. (AFP Photo)
The European Union needs a NATO-like mechanism to better respond to drone incidents, acts of sabotage and cyberattacks across Europe, many of them blamed on Russia, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Sept. 16.
“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook. We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents,” von der Leyen said, particularly for acts that “fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security.”
Officials in Germany, Denmark and Poland have in recent weeks accused Russia of involvement in drone incursions, sabotage, arson, surveillance of defense facilities and planning to use a drone carrying explosives to attack an airport.
Italian fighter jets working with NATO shot down a drone over EU member Lithuania earlier this week, the first time one has been downed in its airspace. It was believed to have entered from Russia’s ally, Belarus.
But Europe and NATO are struggling to know how best to respond to acts that fall short of outright aggression.
Von der Leyen said that the system should be similar to Article 4of NATO’s founding treaty, which allows countries believing that their territory is under threat to convene emergency meetings.
“When triggered by one member state, all member states would convene, to coordinate a European response, to deter further escalation, and to mitigate the impact,” she said.
NATO’s Article 4 is separate from Article 5, the collective security guarantee that obliges all member countries to come to the aid of an ally under attack.
Von der Leyen also said that the EU commission will also “set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality.”
It would involve other international partners like Britain, Canada, Norway and Ukraine, she said, without providing further details.
In her speech, von der Leyen also called for the 27-nation bloc to fight back against “the ultranationalists or the anti-Europeans” who want to undermine it.
“Do we let our democracies be undermined by the proxies and puppets of authoritarians,” von der Leyen asked during a keynote speech to EU lawmakers.
“They despise our values, and they want to shatter our European unity. So let’s not only fight back against that, let’s fight together for our European idea.”
Von der Leyen said the challenges facing Europe, including the cost of living, were fueling “the rise of the extreme, the decline of nuance.”
“These real concerns are being weaponized to drive a wedge between us. Sometimes from the outside, and too often from the inside,” she said.
“But our path is clear: Building an independent Europe that has the power to act. Nothing can divert us from this.”

articles.title: US House takes up Russia sanctions bill backed by late senator Graham
articles.body:
US House takes up Russia sanctions bill backed by late senator Graham
WASHINGTON, Sept 16 - The U.S. House of Representatives is due to vote on Wednesday on a sweeping sanctions bill intended to increase economic pressure on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine, nearly 1-1/2 years after the late Senator Lindsey Graham first introduced it.
The bill, now called the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026" to honor the late South Carolina Republican, passed the Senate last month. House passage would send it to the White House, where President Donald Trump plans to sign it into law.
The legislation would target Russia's energy and defense industries, as well as its "shadow fleet" of tankers that evade existing sanctions.
It also would authorize Trump to impose stiff tariffs on China, India and other countries to reduce their dependence on Russian oil and gas, as well as additional sanctions on Iran.
Supporters expect the House to approve the legislation, even though it has faced considerable opposition since Graham and dozens of other senators introduced it in April 2025. It took Trump until July 2026 — days before Graham's sudden death on July 11 — to allow Congress' Republican leaders to schedule a vote on the bill.
Since starting his second term in January 2025, Trump has generally favored keeping control over tariffs and sanctions, a central tool of his foreign policy, rather than working with Congress on legislation.
The Graham act passed the Senate last month by 86-11 with strong bipartisan support, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy met with lawmakers to urge its passage and took the unusual step of watching an early procedural vote from a seat in the chamber.
KYIV GOVERNMENT URGES PASSAGE
Zelenskiy reiterated his support for the bill in an address this week, saying it is "important that it becomes law. I thank everyone around the world who supports this approach and who knows that strength works," he said.
But it has faced opposition from House Democrats, including some of the chamber's senior leaders, who say the bill gives Trump too many new tariff powers that he could use against U.S. allies. They say Trump already has the authority he needs to impose sanctions on Russia, but has chosen not to do so.
They also say the bill makes it too easy for Trump to waive any sanctions.
"White House lawyers drafted the current text to maximize President Trump’s authority to impose new import taxes on the American people, and to minimize any obligation to actually impose new sanctions on Russia or its enablers," Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, said.
Some Republicans also oppose the bill because they view sanctions as unwarranted intervention in the free market and see U.S. support for Ukraine as contrary to a non-interventionist "America First" view of foreign policy.
Some others also are concerned about political blowback against more tariffs and potentially higher consumer prices ahead of November's midterm elections, in which polls show the party struggling to keep control of the House.
Backers of the bill say it sends an essential message to Russia — and the world — that Washington continues to support Ukraine.
"Putin believes he can keep financing this war indefinitely," said Republican Representative Michael McCaul, a lead sponsor of the bill, of the Russian president. "We need to change that calculation and ensure there are consequences for helping him." REUTERS

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked 15 Chinese military aircraft, eight naval vessels, and two official ships around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Tuesday and 6 a.m. on Wednesday.

Kyiv • UNN
The EU will strengthen its humanitarian, energy and military support for Ukraine. The Union also plans to deliver Patriot missiles and close sanctions loopholes.

articles.title: At least 20 killed after building in Gaza City damaged by Israeli strikes collapses
articles.body:
A building housing about 100 displaced Palestinian families has collapsed in Gaza City, killing at least 20 people, as rescuers search the rubble for dozens of people believed to be trapped, including children.
A rescue team from Gaza’s civil defence said they had recovered the bodies of five children among the victims, while 25 injured people were taken to hospital. Medical sources said rescuers could hear the voices of people trapped beneath the rubble as they tried to reach them.
The bombed-out multi storey building, which contained four apartments on each floor, had previously been hit by Israeli strikes during the war, leaving its structure badly weakened and at risk of collapse. When it gave way on Wednesday, it fell on to tents beside it housing displaced families, witnesses said.
The collapse highlights the continuing danger facing tens of thousands of Palestinians living in an estimated 2,000 buildings damaged by Israeli airstrikes across Gaza.
Mohammed Abu Dan, a superviser with the civil defence team recovering victims, said more than 10 families had been living in the building and displaced people had been forced to stay there because no other shelter was available.
“Search and rescue operations are being carried out under extremely difficult conditions due to a lack of the necessary equipment and resources,” Abu Dan said.
Palestinian and UN officials have blamed Israeli restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery in the territory. Israel says its restrictions are intended to prevent equipment from reaching militant groups.
A video obtained by Reuters showed rescue workers trying to pull two people from beneath a collapsed wall. Another video circulating on social media showed Gaza’s civil defence spokesperson, Mahmoud Basal, carrying a young girl wrapped in a bloodstained scarf.
Raed al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City’s civil defence service, said: “We are still hearing voices from under the rubble, so there is still hope to find people.”
Alessandro Mrakic, the head of the UN Development Programme’s Gaza office, said rescuers from UN agencies were taking part in the operation, which he described as extremely difficult because of the lack of appropriate machinery. Egypt’s relief agency was also involved.
“There are actually people that are digging with their bare hands. We need to prepare [for more deaths],” Mrakic said.
Tents belonging to displaced families had been erected along the road beside the building because there was nowhere else for them to shelter.
Similar incidents have occurred repeatedly over the past two years, with dozens of homes and buildings damaged during the war later collapsing, trapping people and causing further deaths and injuries.
With few other options, many Palestinians have returned to partly destroyed homes or moved into abandoned buildings, clearing small spaces among the rubble despite the danger. Soaring rents and the cost of vacant land have made finding safer accommodation increasingly difficult.
Hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians also remain unable to return to neighbourhoods near the so-called yellow line, forcing families to find whatever space they can elsewhere. In May, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, ordered the military to seize 70% of Gaza.
Damaged roofs, walls and supporting columns can collapse without warning, particularly during strong winds, heavy rain or further bombardment. Asked whether they feared for themselves and their children, people living there said: “Yes, we are afraid, but where can we go? This is better than staying out on the street.”
Israeli strikes on Gaza have continued despite the ceasefire. According to Gaza’s health ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025.
This year, an independent UN inquiry found Israel had continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.
Separately, a video from the Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood of Gaza City showed the aftermath of an Israeli drone strike that killed Mohammed al-Zinati, 15, and wounded several other people. Al-Zinati had been trying to recover the body of a man killed in an earlier strike.
Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said on Wednesday that it was only a matter of time before Israel resumed full-scale war in Gaza and moved to force out its Palestinian population.
Katz, responding to criticism from another rightwing politician before the 27 October elections, said 70% of Gaza had already been emptied of its population during Israel’s offensive launched after the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023 that killed more than 1,200 people, the deadliest attack against Israel, according to official Israeli figures.
He added that the Israel Defense Forces were prepared “to finish the job so that we can also implement the migration plan”.
Since the war began, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the health ministry.

articles.title: Trump administration plans $2.8 billion weapons sale to Israel
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump administration plans to send powerful bombs to Israel in $2.8 billion weapons sale
The Trump administration is planning to deliver powerful 2,000-pound bombs to Israel as part of an upcoming arms deal, weapons that prompted such concerns over mass casualties in Gaza that the Biden administration temporarily paused their delivery two years ago.
The $2.8 billion package includes 40,000 of the bombs, made up of 20,000 Mk84s and 20,000 BLU-117s, according to two US officials and a person familiar with the plan who spoke Tuesday on condition of anonymity to discuss the package, which is not yet final.
Congress has been informally notified about the pending deal, most of which is to be paid for with foreign military financing—in which US taxpayer dollars are given to Israel to turn around and buy the weapons from the United States.
The proposed sale is just the latest in a series of Trump administration steps to improve Israeli’s military capacity. The Israel's genocide of Gaza has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and has decimated the enclave.
The package, which was reported earlier by The Washington Post, comes as Israel has faced increasing international isolation over its genocide.
The sale signals that some strains in the relationship between President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, especially since the two countries launched the war against Iran in February, are not impeding the closeness of the US-Israeli alliance. Trump has had a hot-and-cold history with Netanyahu over the years and expressed some frustration with Netanyahu tied to the Iran conflict before their latest meeting in July at the White House.
In 2024, the Biden administration held off on one shipment of the bombs, but Trump lifted that hold when he took office again.
Last year, the Trump administration bypassed a normal congressional review process and approved a nearly $3 billion sale to Israel that included more than 35,500 of the bombs. The administration then approved a new series of arms sales to Israel totaling $6.67 billion in January.
The 2,000-pound bombs have multiple variants, with some designed to penetrate deep, underground targets while others detonate above ground and cause widespread damage.
Though the Israeli military has offered few details about what bombs and artillery it has used in Gaza, experts analyzing strike footage and blast fragments found on-site believe the US-made bombs have been used there, killing several people in densely populated areas.
While the heaviest fighting in Gaza has subsided since the fragile ceasefire took hold in October, Israel has continued to carry out strikes in the territory, including some overnight and into Tuesday that killed several people. That is even after Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and a key Mideast negotiator, met with Netanyahu last month in an effort to push the ceasefire deal forward and asked Israel to reduce its attacks.

Russian representatives at the IAEA have succeeded in having Crimea designated as Russian territory within the IAEA’s global integrated information system (PRIS) and are demanding further Russification of the names of occupied Ukrainian settlements, according to the Main Intelligence Agency (GUR) of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine.
"For instance, IAEA Deputy Director General Mikhail Chudakov—a Russian national—secured the agency's support for displaying the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea as part of the Russian Federation in the updated IAEA global integrated information system (PRIS)," the GUR stated in a Telegram post regarding the current situation at the Zaporizhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) on Wednesday.

Additionally, the plant is experiencing internet connectivity issues. On August 13–14, 2026, the network was disconnected due to the actions of Russian occupying forces, hindering communication, data monitoring, and international oversight. The Kremlin has also stepped up the implementation of its strategy to integrate the Zaporizhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) into its "legal framework"—specifically, the aggressor state's Federal Service for Environmental, Technological and Nuclear Supervision (Rostekhnadzor) has dispatched a special team of inspectors to the plant.
"At the same time, Moscow is seeking, through its representatives at the IAEA, to russify the organization and leverage the agency's international status to justify the occupation of the ZNPP. One of the objectives of this hybrid campaign is to 'normalize' the information landscape and pave the way for the further legitimization of Russian control over the Ukrainian nuclear power plant," the message notes. As part of these efforts, Russia attempted to orchestrate and exploit for its own ends a visit by IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi to the occupied ZNPP ahead of the 70th session of the IAEA General Conference in Vienna (September 14–17), where the issue of nuclear safety in Ukraine is set to be addressed. articles.title: Iranian pilots narrate how they bombed US base with F-5 jets
articles.body:
Iranian air force pilots said they bombed a key US base with two nearly 70-year-old F-5 fighter jets and destroyed large numbers of American helicopters, in a mission they described as a complete surprise.
The pilots spoke at a meeting with Hojjatoleslam Ahmadreza Pourkhaghan, head of the judicial organisation of the Armed Forces, who attended on behalf of the head of the judiciary ahead of Sacred Defence Week.
The pilots said that after hearing news of the martyrdom of the Leader of the Islamic Revolution and a number of students from Minab, they decided to strike the enemy hard. They said they had information that the enemy had stockpiled large quantities of equipment at one of its important bases in a neighbouring country, and so at dawn on March 1, they were dispatched with two F-5 jets that were nearly 70 years old and considered almost obsolete.
They said that to avoid detection they had to fly at less than 50 feet, about 18 metres above the ground. "The flight altitude was so low that when passing between two ships, the decks of the ships were higher than the fighters," they said.
They said that by God's grace, passing through active Patriot systems and in complete radio silence, they reached the target base in a totally surprising manner, adding that the enemy had not considered such an attack possible.
The pilots said they bombed the helicopters stationed on the flight ramp with full force and destroyed a large number of them. "All of this was God's grace; we clearly saw God's hand in this, because we felt each of our bombs did the work of dozens of bombs, and the helicopters exploded one after another," they said.
They said the enemy admitted to the destruction of only 12 helicopters, but that the real number of destroyed aircraft and casualties was much higher. They said they managed to return to base without the slightest damage.
On the return, they said, an F-16 pursued them, and during this, three American F-15 aircraft that had taken off from a base in another country to attack Iran were mistakenly targeted and shot down by the same F-16 and friendly Patriot systems.
They said that according to an estimate by the AEI think tank, the operation inflicted more than five billion dollars in damage on US infrastructure.
The pilots said the bombing used upgraded, heavy, precise and devastating bombs, and that by God's grace the advanced American helicopters were destroyed in their hangars before any reaction, and the base suffered serious damage.

Anthropic’s Dario Amodei is not the first corporate CEO to suggest that excessive competition is driving the world to some socially undesirable outcome.
The safety breach disclosed by OpenAI after a swarm of its agents coordinated to breach their supposedly secure sandbox, get on the Internet and hack AI platform Hugging Face, warrants urgent action. It demonstrated the ease with which the technology can evade human control and gave concrete form to the existential fears about what it could do to humanity if not securely leashed.
The end of the world may well be nigh, as some in the AI industry have warned. These are truly scary times. But Amodei’s call for the leading artificial intelligence labs to coordinate to slow the breakneck pace of AI development, agree on safety standards and “pace the frontier”, (a call quickly endorsed by Open AI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Google Deep Mind’s Demis Hassabis) is just a hi-tech version of an old proposition by corporate America – to get a pass from antitrust laws designed to protect the American economy from colluding businesses.
It is a dangerous proposition. Freeing the tech bros from antitrust constraints supposedly to allow them to get together and fix AI’s dangerous flaws, disenfranchises the everyday Americans who are most at risk from the thing, further empowering the very labs that, in their pursuit for wealth, greatness and who knows what other fantastical objectives, so casually blew past danger thresholds on many dimensions, bringing the existential threats into being.
Amodei et al’s argument, at heart, is that their businesses are trapped in a prisoner’s dilemma. If they unilaterally slow their fevered pursuit of artificial super-intelligence to make it safer, their rivals – less concerned about existential risks, of course – will get there first, with potentially devastating consequences for humankind, let alone the bottom line of the lab that took its foot off the pedal.
“Slowing down seems sensible,” said Jean Tirole, the Nobel prize-winning economist at the Toulouse School of Economics. “But that assumes coordinated slowing-down is feasible and sustainable. What happens when OpenAI, Anthropic or Grok conclude that US holdouts – or Chinese labs – are catching up? Will they resume immediately, perhaps covertly?”
As Bill Gates has written, “if someone had a credible plan for slowing down AI advances globally, I would likely support it. However, I don’t think that’s going to happen. The geopolitical and economic incentives are pushing too hard to go full speed ahead.” In this light, it might seem like a great idea for the government to encourage a friendly agreement for everybody to slow down. It is not.
The argument that excessive competition is driving a race to the bottom, is probably as old as capitalism, deployed to explain everything from environmental degradation to child labor. But it does not justify giving businesses a right to collude as they see fit. It is a call to craft government regulations to prevent businesses from competing using socially harmful tools.
Moreover, the case that excessive competition is encouraging reckless behavior is dubious. The AI labs are engaged in a winner-takes-all race, one that is extraordinarily expensive to keep going. That’s where the recklessness comes from
Amodei may be an unimpeachable guy. His call to slow the pace of AI development, bring external evaluators into the lab and increase the transparency of his operations suggests sincere concern over the risks. The drop in the price of leading tech stocks following the publication of his propositions suggests that he is willing to take a financial hit in the service of improved safety.
But the investors Amodei hopes will eagerly snap up shares in Anthropic’s IPO later this year may not be so altruistic. Tremors in capital markets suggest that raising the money to finance the trillion-dollar AI investment race is going to get tougher, discouraging strategies that might curb the leading labs’ edge over rivals. Given the incentives, granting the AI leaders a free hand to collude and self-regulate would be foolhardy.
Eric Posner, an antitrust expert at the University of Chicago Law School, said, we “shouldn’t trust companies in general about their motivations”. There is no reason to believe the AI labs, left to their own devices, would necessarily produce good, socially acceptable outcomes. Like any company, they will be calculating trade-offs, weighing risks against profits. And as Posner observed, “they don’t use the same weights as the public”.
So, how to regulate? Nothing is going to happen on this front while Trump is in office. Even after he is gone it will be tough to craft effective regulation to deal with the threats from AI without stunting innovation. There are questions about what rules to deploy, how they are enforced, and who they should apply to. And the peril of unilateral action is real. What if Beijing declines to participate? What are the risks of Chinese AI companies plowing ahead when American labs slow down? But if we could regulate nuclear power, we can probably regulate AI.
Moreover, there are viable ideas that might help even in the absence of government regulation and that don’t require stifling competition. There are proposals to tweak intellectual rights to encourage innovations that improve the safety of AI systems. Inventors of safety innovations would be rewarded by allowing them to release new AI models before their competitors. But the safety enhancements would be made immediately available to all firms.
On the stick side of the ledger, a legal liability regime could be designed to change the incentives of AI developers by punishing firms that gain from the design and deployment of an AI tool that caused harm, even if the harm was unintentional. For instance, the Hugging Face attack might have been prevented if OpenAI’s models had not been inadvertently rewarded for misbehaving during training. The fact that Amodei’s proposal does not mention legal liability suggests that AI leaders’ concern for safety does not override concern for the bottom line.
In any event, cementing in place the dominance of the frontier labs, protecting their rents and endorsing their heretofore gung-ho strategies, is not pro-safety. On the contrary, slowing down the leaders to let the laggards catch up is likely to make the AI ecosystem a safer place by inviting in desirable innovation and promoting competition along the safety dimension.
There is no fundamental conflict between safety and competition. Masters of AI who want to make this case should be viewed with skepticism.

articles.title: US Exposes Russian Spy Network Plotting Killings
articles.body:
US authorities have exposed an alleged Russian intelligence network that recruited operatives to assassinate Kremlin critics in the US and Europe, attacking infrastructure in countries supporting Ukraine.
According to a US Justice Department indictment unsealed on Tuesday, Sept. 15, five suspects allegedly worked for Russian intelligence services to finance terrorism and organize contract killings around the world.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Prosecutors said the network had operated since at least 2024, targeting Russian dissidents and defectors as well as countries considered allies of Ukraine.
“These defendants allegedly operated as part of a global assassination network that reached into the US, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin,” Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg said.
The five defendants remain at large. The indictment constitutes allegations as they are presumed innocent unless proven guilty.
Network allegedly offered $40,000 for US killing
During the summer of 2026, the network allegedly recruited a Venezuelan citizen living in the US to conduct surveillance on a prominent Russian dissident believed to be in the Washington, D.C. area.
The recruit was initially promised between $1,000 and $1,500 to photograph and film two locations associated with the intended victim.
Prosecutors said the network later offered the recruit $40,000 to “eliminate” or “disappear” the dissident. When the recruit refused to personally carry out the killing, alleged network members asked whether he knew “someone [who] can do the work.”
4 Years Since the Discovery of the Izyum Mass Graves
One suspect also claimed that the network had “people in Mexico” who could conduct the assassination.
The group allegedly approached several other people in the US about conducting surveillance and killing the same dissident and other possible targets.
“The Russian-led network charged in today’s indictment is brazen, aggressive, and far-reaching,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald said, adding that law enforcement had “neutralized this deadly and outrageous threat.”
Russian dissident targeted in Lithuania
The network also allegedly attempted to recruit a US citizen in 2025 to surveil and kill a Russian dissident living in Lithuania.
After paying $200 for surveillance, former Russian intelligence colonel Yuri Khrameev allegedly offered the recruit approximately $25,000 to murder the dissident for “telling lies about Russia” and “distorting history.”
Prosecutors said Khrameev proposed killing the victim with a knife or a gasoline bomb.
When the recruit refused, Khrameev allegedly offered a “simpler job” involving setting fire to a warehouse or attacking an electrical substation. He reportedly said the objective was to target “all the countries that are helping Ukraine” and promised “serious money for serious work.”
Five suspects linked to Russian intelligence
The indictment identifies the alleged senior members of the network as:
- Yuri Khrameev, 63, a former colonel in the Russian intelligence services;
- Kirill Khrameev, 27, son of Yuri, and an officer of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB);
- Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35, a Cuban national living in Russia who allegedly coordinated attacks and logistics.
Two alleged recruiters were identified as Cuban national Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35, also known as “Viking,” and Venezuelan national Angel Eduardo Castro, 22.
The Justice Department said Durruthy helped coordinate operations in Prague in June 2024 and Lithuania in September 2024, including arranging travel and sending potential attack locations to other participants.
All five suspects face conspiracy charges related to financing terrorism, carrying a maximum prison sentence of 20 years. Yuri Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro are also charged with conspiracy to commit murder for hire, punishable by up to 10 years.
Wider Russian campaign in Europe
The charges follow a series of investigations into suspected Russian operations targeting critics, infrastructure, and Ukraine’s allies abroad.
In April, Ukrainian prosecutors reported uncovering a separate network linked to Russian security services that was allegedly preparing contract killings, sabotage, and provocations across several European Union countries.
German authorities also recently concluded that Russia was responsible for an attempted explosive drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, prompting Berlin to announce diplomatic and sanctions measures.

articles.title: Zelensky Says Putin Wants All of Ukraine, Rejects ‘Win-Win’ Peace Concept
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russian President Vladimir Putin’s goal in the war extends far beyond seizing additional Ukrainian territory, adding that Moscow ultimately wants Ukraine to become part of Russia.
Speaking to CBC News in an interview, he said Ukraine could accept a ceasefire along the current line of contact if Russia agreed to halt fighting without conditions and the conflict then moved to diplomacy.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are ready for this,” Zelensky said, referring to a potential halt in fighting along the existing front line.
He said negotiations could then continue with the mediation of international partners, adding that a ceasefire without conditions would be preferable to continued fighting.
Zelensky rejects ‘win-win’ concept
Zelensky also rejected the idea that there could be a “win-win” outcome for Russia and Ukraine after the losses caused by the war.
“There is no win-win in this war,” he said, adding that the war ceased to be a situation in which both sides could benefit from the moment it began and caused human casualties.
Zelensky added the most important victory would be to end the war and protect human lives, rather than for either Ukraine or Russia to claim victory.
He acknowledged that he and US presidential envoy Jared Kushner had somewhat different views on the issue but said he was encouraged that Kushner and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff had traveled to Kyiv after multiple visits to Moscow.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 15, 2026
Zelensky said the envoys had asked Ukrainian officials not to publicly discuss some of their proposals while the two sides examined them in greater detail. He added that Ukraine was preparing for a meeting with US President Donald Trump in New York expected later in September.
‘He needs Ukraine’
The Ukrainian president pushed back against the idea that Putin could be satisfied by obtaining a specific portion of Ukrainian territory.
Asked about Kushner’s comments that territory remained a key sticking point and that Putin had outlined the territorial line he wanted, Zelensky said the issue was not simply about “some kilometers” of land.
“The problem is that we have to change Putin’s mind,” Zelensky said.
He argued that it made little sense to suggest Putin needed only a particular part of Ukraine, given that Russia already controls vast territory elsewhere.
“He needs Ukraine,” Zelensky said. “He needs Ukraine [to] be a part of Russia.”
Zelensky said this was why Ukraine could not simply accept a territorial concession as the basis for a lasting settlement.
He also addressed the prospect of meeting Putin directly, saying he was willing to sit across from his adversary if doing so could bring the parties closer to peace.
He acknowledged that such a meeting was not something he personally wanted, saying he would rather spend the time with his family.
“But he is an enemy, of course,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky said he would nevertheless meet Putin if negotiations could produce meaningful progress toward peace. He argued that he understood Putin’s objective and believed the Russian leader would continue trying to occupy Ukraine unless Ukraine remained strong and received credible security guarantees.
“He will not change his goal,” Zelensky said.
For Ukraine, he added, security guarantees would need to ensure that Russia could not simply resume its attempt to occupy the country after a ceasefire or peace agreement.
