articles.title: Russian attacks across Ukraine kill at least 9, injure 36 as drone strike on bus kills 5
articles.body:
Russian attacks across Ukraine kill at least 9, injure 36 as drone strike on bus kills 5
At least nine people were killed and 36 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, including five people killed when a Russian drone struck a passenger bus in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, local authorities said on Sept. 16.
A Russian drone struck a passenger bus in the Nikopol district of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast on the morning of Sept. 16, killing five people at the scene and injuring at least seven others, local Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
"Almost every day, we see Russia striking civilian transport. People who were simply going about their business are killed and injured," Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
In the morning, Preisdent Zelensky said, "Each of these strikes is about the lives of ordinary people who need to be protected by forcing Russia to stop its stupid war."
The morning attack followed another wave of Russian strikes on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast the previous evening. Two people were injured on Sept. 15 as Russian forces attacked three districts more than 10 times with drones, artillery, and aerial bombs, Hanzha added.
Russian forces launched 80 drones overnight, including Shahed-type attack drones, jet-powered variants, Gerbera drones, and decoy drones, the Air Force said. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 63 drones, while strikes were recorded at seven locations. Debris from downed drones fell at two locations, according to the Air Force.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, one person was killed and seven others were injured in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia and the surrounding district, Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the Regional Defense Council, said. Russian forces launched 746 strikes against 52 settlements in the region over the past day, according to Fedorov.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured seven others, regional authorities said. Russian forces targeted critical infrastructure as well as residential areas, damaging three apartment buildings, agricultural machinery and vehicles.
In Donetsk Oblast, two people were killed in Sloviansk and one person was injured in the region over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russian attacks injured 12 people over the past day, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Russian forces used 12 guided aerial bombs, a Geran-2 drone, a Molniya drone, and more than 100 drones of types that authorities were still working to identify, according to Syniehubov.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russian drone attacks damaged 17 sites over the past day and the morning of Sept. 16, with damage recorded in the Bila Tserkva, Boryspil, Brovary, Bucha, and Obukhiv districts, according to local authorities. A driver in the Obukhiv district suffered a concussion from the blast wave after a house, tractor, and vehicle were damaged.

articles.title: Putin weaponizing migration to destabilize Europe, Kyiv says
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking to drive migration to Europe to destabilize governments and weaken support for Ukraine ahead of key upcoming elections, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Sept. 16.
"The Black Sea blockade is part of his plan," Sybiha said, as Russian strikes against ports and vessels in Ukrainian waters are choking off Ukraine's maritime exports, a key source of food for countries across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia.
This strategy not only takes a humanitarian toll on families directly dependent on these supplies, but is also intended to drive an influx of migrants toward the European borders, according to Ukraine's chief diplomat.
"Moscow believes its strategy will create tension, sow division, strengthen radical anti-European movements, and ultimately weaken Europe's support for Ukraine," Sybiha commented on X.
read also
The comments come as the anti-immigration, Russian-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) party secured a historic win in a regional election on Sept. 6, and France's far-right opposition leader Marine Le Pen is a frontrunner for the French presidential run next year.
Next year will also see parliamentary elections in Spain — where the anti-immigration Vox party polls third at around 18% — and in Italy, where right-wing but Ukraine-friendly Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni faces growing pressure from the new far-right National Future movement.
A wave of far-right victories could weaken the support for Ukraine across the European bloc, which has become a key backer of Kyiv after U.S. President Donald Trump cut off much of the American support.
"Putin knows that migration is one of the most sensitive and divisive issues in European election campaigns — especially after seeing how effectively Russian-linked networks exploited the recent Ceuta crisis," Sybiha said.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez previously accused Russian and Israeli disinformation networks of fueling tensions over an August rush of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta.
Next to the Black Sea blockade, Moscow also continues using its ally, Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenko, to smuggle migrants across the EU's northeastern borders, Sybiha added.
While Russia has been striking Ukrainian ports throughout the full-scale war, Kyiv this summer also expanded the list of targets for its drone attacks to Russian ports in the Black and Azov seas, disrupting Russia's own food exports.
The escalation of hostilities in the Black Sea has driven a surge in global food prices, which had already been rising since the start of the U.S.-Iran War in late February.

articles.body:

Ukraine’s SBS Drones Hit 6,280 Russian Troops in 15 Days, Outpacing August Figures
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces reported more than 6,000 confirmed strikes on Russian personnel during the first half of September, surpassing the figure recorded over the same period in August, commander Major Robert “Madyar” Brovdi said on September 16.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Brovdi, Unmanned Systems Forces units killed or incapacitated 6,280 Russian troops during the first 15 days of September, compared with 4,998 over the corresponding period in August.
Brovdi said the largest share of the reported strikes on Russian personnel was recorded in the Dobropillia, Huliaipole, and Pokrovsk sectors. Ukrainian drone units reported 1,806 such strikes in the Dobropillia sector, 1,927 in the Huliaipole sector, and 617 near Pokrovsk.
If the current pace of Russian troop deployments continues and weather conditions remain favorable for drone operations, Brovdi said the monthly figure could reach around 12,500 by the end of September. By comparison, the Unmanned Systems Forces recorded 11,010 confirmed strikes on Russian personnel throughout August.
Brovdi also said Ukrainian drone units expect operations to intensify between October and December, citing anticipated Russian efforts to deploy additional personnel.
“We expect an intensification in October–December 2026 due to the enemy’s intention to deploy an additional 300,000 personnel, which would be exactly twice the previous monthly reinforcement levels,” Brovdi said.
His assessment comes as Russia continues to sustain substantial personnel losses in Ukraine. According to Ukraine’s General Staff, Russian forces recorded 301,030 personnel killed or wounded between the beginning of 2026 and September 15.
To illustrate the scale of the reported losses, the General Staff said the figure is equivalent to the personnel strength of nearly 150 motorized rifle regiments, based on an average of roughly 2,000 troops per brigade.
The heaviest losses were recorded during the summer, when 124,170 Russian troops were reported killed or wounded between June and August. The monthly toll stood at 39,290 in June, increased to 42,860 in July, and reached 42,020 in August.
The losses continued into September, with another 20,360 Russian personnel reported killed or wounded between the beginning of the month and September 15, according to the General Staff.
As Russian battlefield losses continue to mount, Moscow is seeking to expand its military ranks. Russia could mobilize as many as 600,000 additional personnel by the end of 2027 to replenish losses and sustain manpower levels for ongoing offensive operations in Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine ready for energy ceasefire but Russia is yet to agree, Zelenskyy says
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump claimed Moscow and Kyiv have agreed not to target each other’s energy infrastructure, but no deal has been confirmed, and strikes have continued.
Kyiv is ready for an energy ceasefire with Moscow, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, adding that Russia has yet to make the same commitment.
In an interview with CBS, Zelenskyy said US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility during their recent visit to Kyiv. He said Ukraine agreed, on condition that Russia also stops all attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure**.**
“We never attack first. Our tactic is to respond where we can because Putin doesn’t respect and won’t even think of negotiating with weaklings,” Zelenskyy said.
“When Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were here, they proposed thinking about refineries and other energy. I told them we are ready for an energy ceasefire, but you need to know what that means for Ukraine.”
Zelenskyy stressed that an energy ceasefire would have to cover different types of infrastructure: Russian oil and gas facilities targeted by Kyiv, and the electricity and gas infrastructure Moscow has repeatedly struck in Ukraine**.**
“For Putin, energy is selling oil and gas. For us, energy is having electricity and gas supplies for our people,” Zelenskyy said.
“My message was, if the Russians are ready for an energy ceasefire, it means no strikes of any kind with any type of weapon on energy.”
But Moscow is yet to change its tactic. Right after Donald Trump announced the energy truce, the Kremlin-affiliated outlets presented it as a one-way measure, claiming Kyiv will stop its long-range strikes. There was no word regarding Moscow not attacking Ukraine.
The Kremlin has described the proposal as a “very good idea,” but has also linked the wider energy issue to safe commercial shipping, particularly for oil tankers, and the lifting of sanctions on Russia.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian refineries and other oil infrastructure, saying that energy revenues help finance Moscow’s ongoing all-out war.
Russia meanwhile has repeatedly attacked Ukraine’s electricity and gas infrastructure, leaving the country and millions of Ukrainians particularly vulnerable as it prepares for another winter of war.

articles.title: Poroshenko hands over 10 Ai-Petri systems to military
articles.body:
Petro Poroshenko, a Ukrainian MP and leader of the European Solidarity party, announced the handover of another 10 Ai-Petri technical reconnaissance countermeasure systems to Ukraine's Defense Forces.
"The situation on the battlefield has changed. This is not a war of tanks, or even of drones, as we are accustomed to saying. It is now a war of technologies. Whoever leads in technology leads in the war," Poroshenko wrote on Facebook.
According to him, the Ai-Petri system has become one of the most successful Ukrainian defense developments created through private investment.
"Today, we are handing over ten Ai-Petri systems to the Armed Forces. They blind strike drones and prevent them from reaching their targets. Ultimately, this technological advantage is transformed into saved lives of Ukrainian soldiers," he noted.
As reported by the specialized Polish publication Milmag, the Ai-Petri systems were showcased at the MSPO 2026 international security and defense technology exhibition in Kielce, Poland. According to the publication, more than 300 such systems are currently in operation at the front.
According to the manufacturers, Ai-Petri is a system designed to detect and counter enemy technical reconnaissance; it employs machine learning algorithms to adapt to changing battlefield conditions. Upon detecting a target, the system can automatically track it and disrupt its control channels, video transmission, and satellite navigation signals.
According to published specifications, the system is capable of countering targets at ranges of 20 to 30 km, depending on the terrain, and operates within the 300–6000 MHz frequency range. The system is produced in both stationary and mobile versions; the mobile variant can be deployed by two service members in approximately 10 minutes.
The system is also reportedly being deployed to protect critical infrastructure facilities. The Ai-Petri project was launched in the autumn of 2023 with private investment from Poroshenko, who, according to the developers, contributed over UAH 200 million toward its creation and production.

articles.title: Over half of eligible Iranians join Jan Fada campaign
articles.body:
Over half of eligible Iranians join Jan Fada campaign
TEHRAN – The “Jan Fada” (self-sacrificing volunteer) campaign officially launched on March 29 as a spontaneous public movement in response to persistent threats and aggression by the United States and Israel against Iran’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.
More than half of the country’s eligible citizens have registered for the initiative, according to Jan Fada spokesperson Sasan Zare, making it one of the largest public mobilization drives in the country in recent years.
Speaking at a press conference in Tehran on Wednesday, Zare said more than 31.3 million people had registered so far. He described the campaign as an initiative aimed at demonstrating public readiness to defend the country and contribute to various national sectors.
“Of the 31 million people who took part in the campaign, 32 percent were women and 68 percent were men. Notably, the participants were predominantly young, with more than 60 percent under the age of 46,” he said.
According to Zare, 26 percent of volunteers expressed an interest in military and security activities, while 20 percent opted for relief and rescue operations and assistance to those affected. Another 20 percent selected social services, 17 percent volunteered for cultural, artistic, and media activities, and 13 percent offered to provide ongoing financial support. The remaining five percent were classified under miscellaneous services.
Organizers have described Jan Fada as a contemporary expression of Iran’s longstanding tradition of national resilience. The initiative, launched to demonstrate public readiness to defend the country amid heightened geopolitical tensions, quickly attracted millions of registrants nationwide.
The campaign has since expanded from a public registration drive into a broader framework for organized civic participation and national solidarity, bringing together volunteers from diverse communities.
The Jan Fada headquarters has also announced the launch of training and organizational preparations for 1,000 national resistance battalions.
The announcement follows strong public interest and repeated appeals from citizens seeking to stand alongside the country’s armed forces in defending the nation.
According to the organizers, close coordination with military authorities has paved the way for translating the campaign’s broad public participation into structured tactical units.

articles.title: Ukrainian Businesses Expect Hryvnia Revenue Growth, Brace for War Through 2027
articles.body:
Ukraine’s largest businesses expect revenues to continue growing in hryvnia terms next year, even as most see the war extending through 2027.
As companies prepare their 2027 business plans, expectations remain cautious. In hryvnia terms, 53% anticipate revenue growth next year, while 29% expect revenues to decline and 18% foresee no change from 2026. In US dollar terms, however, sentiment is less optimistic: 41% expect revenues to fall, 36% predict growth, and 23% expect them to remain stable.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The findings, drawn from the European Business Association’s (EBA) annual survey of member-company CEOs, capture a corporate sector that has learned to operate in a wartime environment with no clear end in sight. Nearly all respondents (98%) are budgeting for continued fighting in 2027, yet companies continue to invest, adopt artificial intelligence tools, and fund social initiatives, suggesting that the war has not derailed their long-term priorities. That being said, 38% expect output or sales volumes to decline in 2027, 35% predict growth, and 27% anticipate no change.
Despite the caution, some companies are still planning to expand. About 3% of respondents intend to launch new large-scale investment projects in 2027, with an average expected price tag of around $5 million.
“Business today operates under increasing pressure from enemy strikes,” the EBA quoted its executive director, Anna Derevyanko, as saying in a press release.

“Therefore, it is quite logical that among the main tasks for the government of the company are the protection of business assets and strengthening energy sustainability. This is an important signal: even in the conditions of war, business does not lose focus on systemic changes, without which the long-term development of the economy and the recovery of the country are impossible.”

Meanwhile, labor shortages continue to drive digital transformation. In 2027, 83% of companies expect to deploy artificial intelligence tools to automate processes, boost productivity, and offset workforce constraints.
Willingness to fund social initiatives remains even higher. Nearly half of the surveyed companies (48%) plan to invest in social projects in 2027, with such spending averaging around 4% of company revenue.

The Trump administration is stripping tens of millions of dollars in US military assistance from countries in Europe and the Middle East to support conservative-leaning governments in Central and South America.
The State Department on Tuesday notified Congress that it will reprogram $52 million in foreign military financing from Slovakia, North Macedonia, Tunisia and Iraq to Panama, Peru, Ecuador and Colombia.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Colombia, Ecuador and Peru last week and pledged to them additional support as the Trump administration has prioritized the Western Hemisphere in its foreign policy with an emphasis on combating drug trafficking and illegal immigration.
It is just the latest in a series of moves that have reduced either money or troop deployments to Europe in response to President Donald Trump's complaints about NATO allies not spending enough on their defense budgets and other matters. Both North Macedonia and Slovakia are NATO members.
But it also comes as the administration has put particular attention on the Western Hemisphere, aligning deeply with right-wing governments as Trump celebrates a renewal of the 19th century Monroe Doctrine establishing Washington's dominance in the Americas.
Foreign military financing provides recipient countries with US taxpayer dollars to allow them to purchase military equipment from American defense contractors.
The State Department said the funds would be used to "combat narcoterrorism in our backyard and help continue to secure the Panama Canal," adding that the Western Hemisphere has been historically neglected in US military assistance.
"These funds will prevent adversaries from establishing strategic footholds in our hemisphere," the department said in a veiled jab at China, which has increasingly sought to boost its presence in Latin America.
The shift of money does not eliminate foreign military financing for Tunisia, Iraq, North Macedonia or Slovakia, although the exact amount remaining for those countries was not immediately clear.
The State Department said, though, that the current distribution of financing does "not align with the administration’s prioritisation of" the Western Hemisphere.

articles.title: Russian general killed in Ukraine weeks after telling Putin Kostiantynivka was captured
articles.body:
Russian Major General Anton Grunis, the commander who told Russian President Vladimir Putin that Russian forces had fully captured Kostiantynivka despite Ukrainian troops still defending the city, has been killed in the war against Ukraine, according to Russian media reports.
Grunis was awarded the Hero of Russia title just weeks before his death, after commanding Russian forces on the Kostiantynivka front. He had reported the city’s supposed capture to Putin in July, even as Ukrainian forces continued to hold positions there.
Robert “Madyar” Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (SBS), confirmed Grunis’s death on 16 September, saying Ukrainian forces killed the general on 12 September in occupied Donetsk Oblast.
Madyar said the operation was carried out by the “Rarog” unit of Ukraine’s 427th Separate Regiment of Unmanned Systems.
Several Russian sources have also confirmed Grunis’s death, according to Ukrainska Pravda and RBC-Ukraine.
Madyar said Grunis is the seventh confirmed Russian commander at the brigade, division, or army level killed by Ukraine’s SBS “Birds” units.
The general who declared Kostiantynivka captured
Grunis commanded Russia’s 4th Separate Guards Motor Rifle Brigade, which has been fighting on the Kostiantynivka front, according to Ukrainska Pravda.
In July, Grunis personally reported to Putin that Russian forces had supposedly fully captured Kostiantynivka. Russia’s Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov made a similar claim.
Ukraine rejected the announcement, saying its troops were still conducting defensive operations inside the city. Kostiantynivka remains contested as of 16 September.
RBC-Ukraine reported that Russian troops have entered parts of the city, but Ukrainian forces continue to hold positions in its southern, central, and northern areas. Ukraine’s General Staff reported 18 Russian attacks on the Kostiantynivka axis over the previous day.
Kostiantynivka is the southernmost major city in Ukraine’s fortified defensive belt in Donetsk Oblast, with Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk, and Sloviansk farther north. Russia has been trying to capture it since 2025.
Kostiantynivka: Why one city in Donbas matters so much that Putin lies about having captured it
Killed weeks after receiving Hero of Russia title
Grunis was awarded Russia’s highest state decoration shortly before his death. On 27 August, Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov presented him with the Gold Star of the Hero of the Russian Federation for what Russia described as his “courage and heroism,” according to Ukrainska Pravda.
Grunis graduated from the Kazan Suvorov Military School in 1996 and fought in Chechnya and against Georgia, Ukrainska Pravda reported. He retired from active service in 2021 but returned to the Russian military after the start of the full-scale invasion.
The 4th Separate Guards Motor Rifle Brigade was formed in 2014 from Russian-backed armed formations in occupied Luhansk, including the Prizrak group, before being integrated into Russia’s regular military structure, according to Ukrainska Pravda.

articles.title: Russian authorities order destruction of vaccine batch linked to mass dog deaths
articles.body:
Russian authorities order destruction of vaccine batch linked to mass dog deaths
Rosselkhoznadzor, Russia’s Federal Service for Veterinary and Phytosanitary Surveillance, has ordered the recall and destruction of batch No. 20 of the “Multikan-8” vaccine, which has been linked to dog deaths. The agency sent the order in a letter (.pdf) to the vaccine’s manufacturer, the company “Vetbiokhim,” and published the document on its website.
The letter directs “Vetbiokhim” to recall and destroy batch No. 20 itself, then report back to Rosselkhoznadzor.
Why Rosselkhoznadzor ordered the destruction of only one batch of “Multikan” remains unclear. “Vetbiokhim” had already recalled four batches of the vaccine amid earlier reports of mass dog deaths following vaccination.
Dog deaths after vaccination with "Multikan"
Dog owners began speaking out in large numbers in mid-August about pets that died after being vaccinated with “Multikan-8,” saying at least 300 animals died across several Russian regions. Those affected asked lawmakers in the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, to look into what happened.
No official figures on the number of dogs that died exist, and it’s unclear whether such statistics were ever compiled. Rosselkhoznadzor’s regional office and the prosecutor’s office in the Yaroslavl region, where the first reports of dog deaths surfaced, launched an inspection of “Vetbiokhim,” though no results have been announced.
Some of those affected (1, 2, 3) have linked the deaths to contamination of the “Multikan-8” vaccine with the virus that causes Aujeszky’s disease (pseudorabies), whose symptoms resemble those seen in the dogs that died. Unofficial testing of vaccine samples allegedly also detected the virus, according to those affected, but laboratories soon began refusing to run the tests, citing “pressure from above.”
“Vetbiokhim” claimed its own tests had found no contamination of the vaccine with the Aujeszky’s disease virus.
On September 10, Meduza reported that “Vetbiokhim” had drawn up settlement agreements with those affected. The company did not acknowledge any link between the dog deaths and the vaccine but offered to compensate the owners of animals that died. The agreements, however, required owners to waive any claims against “Vetbiokhim” and to stop discussing what happened to their animals in the media, on social media, or in messaging apps without the company’s consent.
“Multikan-8” is a vaccine that protects dogs against canine distemper, adenovirus infections, parvovirus and coronavirus enteritis, leptospirosis, and rabies.
Imported veterinary drugs, including rabies vaccines, largely vanished from the Russian market after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the Western sanctions that followed, leaving veterinary clinics to rely mostly on Russian-made products.

articles.title: JD Vance: US cannot be ‘subservient’ to Israel on Middle East policy
articles.body:
U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Washington cannot allow its Middle East policy to be “subservient to the State of Israel,” in a blunt assertion about a key regional ally from one of the Trump administration’s top figures and a leading 2028 Republican presidential contender.
Speaking Tuesday at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles, Vance said Israel remained an important partner on military technology and intelligence, but that the U.S. would not automatically follow the Israeli government’s lead on security issues.
“We’re going to work with people when we work with them. We’re going to disagree when we disagree. And we’re going to pursue America’s interests,” Vance said.
Advertisement
The Trump administration and Israel launched an attack on Iran on Feb. 28 — sparking an ongoing war in the Middle East, which has driven up energy prices and stifled marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital chokepoint for the transport of fuel.
The Israeli parliament hailed U.S. President Donald Trump last year, for America’s role in releasing hostages held by Palestinian militants in Gaza. On March 5, Defense Minister Israel Katz thanked Trump for his “great support for Israel” and said cooperation between Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was “changing regional and global history.”
That optimism masks an increasingly complicated relationship. In June, Vance warned Israel that it had few friends left and should think carefully before alienating Washington.
The U.S. vice president already angered parts of Israel’s diplomatic community — as well as the pro-Israel Republican establishment. His defense in June of a ceasefire agreement with Iran rattled Israeli officials and damaged his standing with some pro-Israel Republican donors.
In Tuesday’s remarks, he also praised Trump for being willing to break with Netanyahu when American and Israeli interests diverged.
“Donald Trump is the one president of the last 40 years who’s been willing to say ‘You know what, yeah Bibi’s a good partner, but also Bibi and I have a different opinion on this,’ or ‘Bibi’s wrong about this,’ or maybe ‘Bibi’s right about this from the perspective of Israel, but the American people need us to go in a different direction,’” he said.
Vance also compared the relationship with Israel to Washington’s European alliances, saying U.S. policy should not be “subservient to NATO” either.

articles.title: The ‘Ossoff angle’: media-savvy senator borrows from Obama as 2028 chatter builds
articles.body:
Delivering a speech in Atlanta last month, Jon Ossoff accused Donald Trump of corruption, incompetence and fecklessness, and peppered his remarks with substantive observations of dates and times and places. But the comment that ricocheted across the internet – a clip of just a few seconds – was an almost-throwaway reference about how the US president wants to “travel with Natalie” onboard Air Force One.
The crowd cheered the US senator, who is running for re-election in battleground Georgia and is increasingly seen as a potential Democratic candidate for president in 2028. But his target audience that day – and this year – spanned far beyond the concert hall.
After his remark went viral, stories about Trump’s young, exceptionally devoted, presidential aide Natalie Harp rippled through social and established media. Often enough, they were accompanied by an image of Ossoff, his sharp jawline captured from below as he looks into the middle distance.
This photographic framing has increasingly been referred to as the “Ossoff angle”, perhaps in a disservice to myriad politicians from John F Kennedy to Barack Obama who also employed the technique, snapped at a low angle from a camera pit over the past century.
While the approach is not new, it has helped the senator for Georgia to reach the social media feeds of users far beyond his state.
Kathleen Hall Jamieson, professor of communication at Penn’s Annenberg School, likened Ossoff to Kennedy. The first millennial senator has mastered the medium of the moment, she suggested, much as Kennedy was the first president who really understood television.
“How do you communicate that this is a new generation of leadership?,” Jamieson asked. “And how do you do that rhetorically? Because you can’t just stand up and say, ‘This is a new generation of leadership.’
“You have to have people draw that conclusion about you. And part of the way you do that is you master the media of the time, and you demonstrate that in the process you have leadership capacity and that you have the capacity to deal with the old order.”
At 33 years, 11 months and four days, Ossoff was the youngest US senator sworn into the 117th Congress. At 39 today, and ever so slightly gray at the temple, he remains the youngest in a chamber with an average age of 65.
The value of good lighting, a good background and a good angle in a social media post is not lost on a film-maker, as Ossoff was before turning to public office. The former documentarian has a knack for winning the algorithm with plain language, surfacing absurdities in an era of absurdities.
While Trump is also a master of social media, the effect is different. His audience is generationally different.
Trump, who regularly attaches infantile nicknames to his political enemies as a political marketing gimmick, calls Ossoff “Pee-wee Herman”, a tepid sobriquet which hasn’t yet landed.
More recently, the Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican-aligned Super Pac, began running ads about Ossoff’s haircare and makeup regime using AI-generated videos of Ossoff in a salon chair. (Ossoff has spent about $1,200 on hair and makeup this election cycle – a drop in the bucket, given a fundraising haul of $81m up to June, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) disclosures.)
Georgia elected Ossoff in a nail-biting runoff in January 2021 with control of the Senate on the line, amid the turmoil of Trump’s election dispute. His election, alongside fellow Georgia Democrat Raphael Warnock, secured the Senate majority for Democrats. Rioters stormed the US Capitol the next day.
Since taking office, Ossoff has built a high profile as an opponent of Washington corruption, maladministration and the so-called Epstein class. He grilled CIA director John Ratcliffe after Jeffrey Goldberg, the editor-in-chief of the Atlantic, published a report that senior officials had shared sensitive information about future military strikes on Signal with him. He pressed Russ Vought, Trump’s budget director, after massive cuts to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. He questioned former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard on her presence at an FBI raid that seized 2020 ballots in Fulton county.
His questioning of such Trump administration officials have proven as likely to reach wide social media audiences as anything he says on the campaign trail.
Clips circulated of Ossoff repeatedly pressing intelligence director nominee Jay Clayton during a July 2026 hearing to say plainly whether the 2020 election was legitimate. Ossoff’s questions left Clayton sitting in silence at the hearing table, refusing to speak. “Your answers lack credibility,” Ossoff declared. “Your testimony lacks credibility. You’re being evasive and you’re not being candid or forthright. And everybody across the country is going to watch this and know that.”
But outside of the spotlight, Ossoff has held hearings on child welfare and federal prison abuses both in Washington DC and across the state of Georgia. These relatively quiet issues tend to draw little media attention and less financial interest from funders, though they are a vital element of government oversight.
“It is clear that Jon Ossoff believes what he is saying, and people – they get it,” said Charlie Bailey, chairman of Georgia’s Democratic party. “And so it not only matches up with their experience and their their anger and their frustration, they know he’s telling the truth. They know he’s saying what he believes, and that’s why he’s saying it, because he thinks it’s the right thing to do.”

articles.title: Five killed in Russian drone strike on bus in southern Ukraine
articles.body:
The United Nations says civilian deaths in Ukraine are running at their highest level since the first months of the war.

articles.title: Israel’s F-35 jets are getting a new precision weapon
articles.body:
- Rafael announced Sept. 15, 2026, that it is integrating its SPICE 1000 precision-guided munition onto the F-35 Adir for the first time.
- The work is a joint project with Lockheed Martin carried out in the United States, building on years of SPICE 1000 use aboard Israeli F-15 and F-16 jets.
Rafael Advanced Defense Systems is integrating its SPICE 1000 precision-guided munition onto the F-35 Adir fighter jet for the first time, the Israeli company announced Sept. 15, 2026, at the AFA Air, Space & Cyber conference.
The work is being carried out jointly with Lockheed Martin at Lockheed’s facilities in the United States.
SPICE 1000 is a 453 kg (1,000-pound) class guidance kit that converts standard bombs into precision, stand-off weapons capable of hitting fixed and high-value targets from more than 120 km (75 miles) away. It uses an electro-optical seeker paired with scene-matching algorithms, letting it lock onto a target by comparing what it sees to stored imagery rather than relying solely on GPS, a feature designed to keep the weapon accurate even in environments where satellite navigation is jammed or unavailable.
The Israeli Air Force has flown SPICE 1000 for years, primarily on its F-15 and F-16 fleets, and the weapon has been a mainstay of the service’s long-range strike missions. Rafael and Lockheed Martin first signed an agreement to jointly market SPICE kits internationally in 2018, and the two companies have said publicly for several years that F-35 integration was on their roadmap. This week’s announcement marks the point where that integration work has moved forward on the F-35 platform specifically.
SPICE is manufactured in three weight classes: SPICE 1000, SPICE 2000, and the smaller SPICE 250, all sharing a stand-off range of up to 120 km. The family has been sold to multiple air forces beyond Israel and has been integrated on other fighter types, including the Saab Gripen. Rafael has said the SPICE program has won Israel’s Defense Prize.
Because the F-35’s internal weapons bays are limited in size and shape, integrating an existing munition onto the jet typically requires software, wiring and structural work to confirm the weapon fits, communicates with the aircraft’s systems and can be released safely, a process distinct from simply mounting a bomb onto an external pylon.
Neither company disclosed a timeline for completing that work on SPICE 1000, nor did they specify whether the integration covers internal carriage, external carriage, or both.

There Can’t Be “Win-Win in This War” After Years of Human Losses, Zelenskyy Says
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said there can no longer be a “win-win” outcome to Russia’s war against Ukraine after years of human losses, arguing that the priority should now be stopping the war and preserving lives.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking in an interview with CBC News, Zelenskyy rejected the idea that an end to the war could produce an outcome equally beneficial to Ukraine and Russia. “Between us, there can be no win-win in this war. After so many human losses, it stopped being about victory for both sides on the very first day,” Zelenskyy said.
He argued that the only meaningful outcome now would be to stop the war in order to save lives rather than search for a formula in which both sides emerge as winners.
Zelenskyy’s comments followed remarks by Jared Kushner during a September 6 visit to Kyiv, where he described the US approach to international negotiations, including efforts to end Russia’s war against Ukraine, as based on a “win-win” concept.
Kushner said the US negotiating team was approaching the issue from a business perspective and looking for an outcome that could create benefits for both sides. Zelenskyy also disputed the view that Russian leader Vladimir Putin could be satisfied with gaining only additional Ukrainian territory.
“He has the largest territory in the world, and he needs some kilometers? That is why it is very strange when some partners say: he only needs this part of Ukraine, these kilometers, and that’s it,” Zelenskyy said.
According to the Ukrainian president, Putin’s objectives extend beyond individual regions or territorial concessions. Zelenskyy said Moscow ultimately seeks to bring all of Ukraine under Russian control.
Ukraine and the United States remain in regular contact over efforts to end the war, Zelenskyy said. He added that Washington had asked Kyiv not to publicly disclose details of proposals currently under discussion while the sides continue working on them.
Zelenskyy also called for stronger US sanctions aimed at reducing Russia’s ability to continue the war.
Ukraine and the US are now preparing for a meeting between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump in New York later in September, potentially on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

China Builds World’s First Mothership to Deploy Giant Submarine Drones
China is accelerating its naval modernization with the construction of what appears to be the world’s first mothership designed to deploy full-sized uncrewed submarines, Naval News reported on September 15.
Spotted at the Hudong-Zhonghua shipyard in Shanghai, the specialized vessel marks a significant milestone in Beijing’s undeclared initiative to operationalize extra-extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicles (XXLUUVs).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to satellite imagery reviewed by Naval News, the new vessel resembles an amphibious landing ship equipped with a stern well-deck. Unlike standard well-decks, this design is open underneath and utilizes a large cradle on 12 vertical “jack-up” arms to deploy and recover the drones.
Forward of the well-deck, an internal hangar provides space to house the submersibles. Given the dimensions of the Chinese XXLUUVs, the mothership is estimated to be capable of carrying up to four of the massive drones simultaneously.
China is currently the only nation building full-size autonomous submarines. Two models, measuring between 35 and 45 meters (115–148 feet) in length, are undergoing testing in Hainan. These Chinese platforms are roughly six to eight times larger than the US Navy’s Boeing Orca XLUUV, according to Naval News.
Until now, the Chinese Navy has relied on specially designed floating docks for coastal testing, making the introduction of a mobile, deep-water mothership a critical upgrade for operational deployment.
While the new ship’s design shares similarities with a 2025 proposal for a civilian undersea research submersible, its sheer scale and the inclusion of a closed internal hangar strongly indicate a military application. Naval News assessed that the only plausible role for the vessel is as a drone submarine tender and combat launch platform.
The exact strategic doctrine for China’s XXLUUV fleet remains undisclosed. However, the drones are expected to fulfill long-range combat roles, which could include autonomous deployments off the west coast of the United States during periods of heightened tension. This dedicated infrastructure investment indicates that Beijing is pushing well ahead of global competitors in integrating uncrewed platforms into deep-water naval operations.
Meanwhile, the evolution of uncrewed naval capabilities is already transforming active combat zones. In the Black Sea, Ukrainian forces recently recorded what is considered the first naval battle in history between two uncrewed surface vessels. A Ukrainian Sargan-3000 maritime drone, equipped with a remote-controlled 12.7 mm machine gun turret, successfully intercepted a Russian surface drone.
After targeting the Russian vessel’s communication antennas from approximately one kilometer away to disrupt its remote control, the Ukrainian drone immobilized and sank the target.

Russia sentences professor with dual Russian-Canadian citizenship to seven years for treason
The Supreme Court of the Komi Republic sentenced Nikolai Zyuzev, a Russian and Canadian citizen, to seven years in prison on charges of preparing a “project against Russia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity” using foreign grants.
Zyuzev developed the project and began implementing it in February 2022, according to Russia’s Federal Security Service, as cited by the Russian state news agency TASS. The project called for, among other things, “training abroad leaders of national liberation movements of Russia’s small indigenous peoples.”
Zyuzev received a total of $2 million for the project from 12 foreign organizations, including some designated as “undesirable,” the security service announced. “Zyuzev fully admitted guilt in the crime he was charged with and exposed the people involved in it,” the FSB claimed.
Zyuzev holds a doctorate in philosophy, the Russian Telegram news channel Ostorozhno Novosti reported. He taught at institutions of higher education in Komi, including heading the philosophy department at Ukhta State Technical University.
In 2008, Zyuzev moved to Canada, where he earned a law degree and taught at a college affiliated with the University of Toronto.
He returned to Syktyvkar in 2015 and resumed teaching. After the start of the full-scale war, Zyuzev left Russia but continued to visit Komi. He has been in custody since June 2026.

“Today, there was a report from the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Mykhailo Drapatyi, about a new step by our manufacturers: there has been a successful test of another interceptor against Russian jet drones. The Shahed was successfully hit,” the President stated.
He added that the project is currently being refined and that work by other developers is also ongoing.
"We are awaiting a functional tool. It is crucial to have a sufficient range of defenses against attack drones. We are currently deploying our combat aircraft—fighters and helicopters—to the fullest extent to provide cover for cities and villages. The interceptor crews tasked with taking down standard 'Shaheds' are operating effectively; last night, the shoot-down rate for Shaheds was 93 percent. That is a significant figure, though, of course, more is needed. We are allocating whatever state resources and funds are required for this effort to ensure the provision of all necessary weaponry," Zelenskyy concluded.

articles.title: What von der Leyen’s words reveal about the mood in the EU
articles.body:
Europe is at a “tipping point,” according to Ursula von der Leyen.
In her State of the Union address on Wednesday, the Commission president warned that the bloc had reached a watershed moment on several levels — from trade with China to climate change and artificial intelligence.
The EU is “the strongest it has ever been,” even though it could equally “feel as precarious as it has ever been,” said von der Leyen.
Advertisement
POLITICO analysis of the speech shows that commonly mentioned themes included Ukraine, threats to defense and security, energy prices and artificial intelligence, as well as this summer’s heat waves and pressure on the bloc’s external borders.
Faced with Russian strikes on Ukrainian cities, a surge of migrants into the Spanish territory of Ceuta that laid bare EU divisions on migration, and with devastating wildfires and droughts that affected much of the Continent, the bloc had lived through a “summer of truth,” according to the Commission chief.
“There can be no repeat of this summer,” she said.
Comparing this year’s speech with past addresses shows how the major threads in the annual State of the Union have evolved.
They moved from the Greek debt crisis and upsurge in refugee arrivals in 2015, under former Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker, to the Green Deal in 2020, at the start of von der Leyen’s first term, to a focus on Russia, Ukraine, energy, security and defense now.

articles.title: Zelensky: Energy ceasefire means no attacks on facilities with any type of weapon
articles.body:
Zelensky: Energy ceasefire means no attacks on facilities with any type of weapon
He made these remarks in an interview with CBS, according to Ukrinform, citing the head of state’s Telegram channel.
“The inability to transport oil and sell it is a major blow to the Russian budget—more than 100 billion a year. This year it will be even more—150 billion. We never strike first. Our tactic is to respond where we can, because Putin does not respect the weak and would not even consider negotiating with them,” Zelensky said.
According to him, when U.S. President’s special representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were in Ukraine, they suggested “thinking about oil refineries and other energy infrastructure.”
“I told them that we are ready for an energy ceasefire, but we need to understand what that means for Ukraine. For Putin, energy means selling oil and gas. For us, energy means electricity and gas for our people. My message was this: if the Russians are ready for an energy ceasefire, that means no attacks on energy infrastructure with any type of weapon,” the head of state said.
The president added that there should be no blockade on agricultural exports, because this is a matter of food security for many people on other continents.
“Russia has up to 70 million metric tons of agricultural products for sale. Ukraine needs to sell about 30 million. This is also in their interest,” he said.
The head of state noted: if the Russian side does not plan to attack certain targets, then it must present a list of its own targets—those it does not want the Ukrainian side to attack.
“Even during a war, it is possible to find opportunities for de-escalation. If you are negotiating, it means you are demonstrating goodwill or the political will to end the war,” Zelensky emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that he hopes to meet with U.S. President Donald Trump in New York next week. According to him, the key topics will be a maritime and energy truce.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha emphasized that Ukraine is ready for an energy truce and hopes that the joint efforts of international partners will lead to its achievement.

articles.title: Four years after Mahsa Amini's death, rights groups warn Tehran's crackdown persists
articles.body:
Human rights groups said those who directed the violent suppression of the 2022 protests still control Iran's security apparatus, as Kurdish businesses shuttered across her home region and the UN Special Rapporteur said four years of state violence had failed to extinguish the resistance.
Four years after the death of Mahsa Amini in Iranian police custody, Kurdish businesses across her home region staged a general strike on Wednesday while international human rights organisations warned that those responsible for crushing the 2022 protests remain in power and continue to use the same methods.
Shopkeepers and businesses in Saqqez, Sanandaj, Mahabad, Marivan, Baneh and Bokan shut their doors following a call by Kurdish political coalitions. Video circulating on social media showed empty bazaars across the region.
Amnesty International, in a report marking the fourth anniversary, said those who directed the violent suppression of the 2022 protests still control Iran's security apparatus.
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola (Malta/EPP) said on X that the Parliament would continue to support young Iranians facing execution or imprisonment, singling out the case of twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, sentenced by Tehran's Revolutionary Court after recent protests.
The European Parliament "will keep their light shining until it breaks through the darkness.", Metsola wrote on X.
UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights in Iran Mai Sato said that four years of brutal state violence — including lethal force deployed during nationwide protests in late 2025 and early 2026 — have failed to extinguish the resistance.
"Four years on, the resistance Jina’s death gave rise to has not been extinguished," Sato said in a statement on X.
"The women and girls who took to the streets in her name still insist on the right to decide what they wear, where they work and how they live... Those rights will not stay deniable forever."
Sato also noted that despite the Law on Protecting the Family through the Promotion of the Culture of Chastity and Hijab being formally suspended since December 2024, cafes, restaurants and shops have continued to be closed for hijab violations, with arrests reported in some cases.
What happened to Mahsa Amini?
Amini, 22, was detained by Tehran's morality police on 13 September 2022 over compulsory hijab rules and died three days later after being brutally beaten in custody.
The UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran concluded she had been subjected to physical violence in custody and that Iranian authorities were responsible for her death. Iranian officials rejected the findings and denied she had been physically assaulted.
Protests spread nationwide in the days after her death. While compulsory hijab and women's rights were central, the movement drew together demands for political freedoms, minority rights, economic justice and changes to the political system.
The UN fact-finding mission documented up to 551 deaths across 26 provinces, including at least 49 women and 68 children, and said some violations — including killings, torture, rape and sexual violence — reached the threshold of crimes against humanity.
Tehran acknowledged detaining more than 22,000 people, according to Amnesty International, which also documented enforced disappearances, unfair trials and death sentences.
Tehran pivots to hi-tech
Compulsory hijab remains law, the political structure is intact, and many participants in the protests are in prison, in exile or under sentence.
The regime has shifted enforcement away from morality-police patrols toward cameras, facial recognition, drones and digital tools. Iran's police announced in 2023 that public cameras would be used to identify women not wearing hijab.
The UN fact-finding mission's 2025 report cited facial recognition being used to monitor students' dress at the entrance to Amirkabir University in Tehran.
A 2025 study published in the journal Iranian Studies at the University of Cambridge described the movement as producing a "cultural revolution" alongside a political one, arguing it weakened the state's ideological hold over public and cultural life.
For instance, images of morality police vans detaining women on the streets were among the most potent symbols of the 2022 protests, prompting Tehran to avoid public confrontation methods.
The growing presence of women without headscarves in public spaces and the central place women's rights and freedoms take in political debate show that the situation has not reverted to where it stood before September 2022 — a direct result of the movement's actions.
